chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Alexandria. A Room in Cleopatra’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter DEMETRIUS and PHILO.]

PHILO. No, this infatuation of our general's has gone way too far. Those magnificent eyes of his, which used to glow like armored Mars surveying the ranks and assemblies of war, now bend their gaze and devote their attention to a swarthy face. That captain's heart, which in the scuffles of great battles burst the buckles on his breastplate, has abandoned all restraint and become the bellows and the fan to cool a gypsy's lust.
[A flourish of trumpets. Enter ANTONY and CLEOPATRA, her ladies-in-waiting, the train, with eunuchs fanning her.]
Look, here they come. Just watch closely, and you'll see in him the triple pillar of the world transformed into a whore's fool. Behold and see.
CLEOPATRA. If it really is love, tell me how much.
ANTONY. There's poverty in a love that can be measured.
CLEOPATRA. I'll set a limit on how far I'm to be loved.
ANTONY. Then you'll have to discover a new heaven and a new earth.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. News, my good lord, from Rome.
ANTONY. It annoys me — get to the point.

CLEOPATRA. No, hear them out, Antony. Fulvia may be angry; or who knows whether the barely-bearded Caesar hasn't sent you his powerful command: "Do this or that; take that kingdom and free this one. Carry it out, or else we'll condemn you."
ANTONY. What, my love?

CLEOPATRA. Perhaps! No, more than likely. You can't stay here any longer; your dismissal has come from Caesar — therefore hear it, Antony. Where's Fulvia's summons? — Caesar's, I should say? Both? Call in the messengers. As I am Egypt's queen, you're blushing, Antony, and that blood of yours pays tribute to Caesar; or else your cheek pays the price of shame when shrill-tongued Fulvia scolds you. The messengers!

ANTONY. Let Rome dissolve into the Tiber, and the wide arch of the assembled empire fall! Here is my place. Kingdoms are clay. Our dung-heap earth feeds beast and man alike. The noble thing in life is to do this [embracing her]; when such a mutual pair and such a couple can do it — on pain of punishment, I bind the world to acknowledge we stand unmatched.
CLEOPATRA. What excellent lying! Why did he marry Fulvia, and not love her? I'll pretend to be the fool I'm not. Antony will be himself.

ANTONY. But only when stirred by Cleopatra. Now, for the love of Love itself and her soft hours, let's not waste the time on harsh conversation. There's not a minute of our lives that should pass without some pleasure now. What entertainment tonight?
CLEOPATRA. Hear the ambassadors.

ANTONY. For shame, you quarrelsome queen! Everything becomes you — to scold, to laugh, to weep; every passion of yours strives fully to make itself, in you, beautiful and admired! No messenger but yours, and tonight, all alone, we'll wander through the streets and observe the manners of the common people. Come, my queen, last night you wanted to. Don't speak to us.
[Exeunt ANTONY and CLEOPATRA with the Train.]
DEMETRIUS. Is Caesar valued so cheaply by Antony?
PHILO. Sir, sometimes, when he isn't being Antony, he falls short of that great quality that ought to belong to Antony.
DEMETRIUS. I'm sorry indeed that he confirms the common gossip that speaks of him this way in Rome — but I'll hope for better deeds tomorrow. Rest in peace!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Alexandria. Another Room in Cleopatra’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter ENOBARBUS, a Soothsayer, CHARMIAN, IRAS, Mardian and Alexas.]

CHARMIAN. Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, all-things Alexas, almost completely absolute Alexas, where's that soothsayer you praised so highly to the queen? Oh, if only I knew this husband who, you say, must crown his horns with garlands!
ALEXAS. Soothsayer!
SOOTHSAYER. What do you want?
CHARMIAN. Is this the man? Are you the one, sir, who knows things?
SOOTHSAYER. In nature's infinite book of secrets I can read a little.
ALEXAS. Show him your hand.
ENOBARBUS. Bring in the banquet quickly — wine enough to drink Cleopatra's health.
CHARMIAN. Please, sir, give me good fortune.
SOOTHSAYER. I don't make it, I foresee it.
CHARMIAN. Please then, foresee me a good one.
SOOTHSAYER. You'll be far more beautiful than you are now.
CHARMIAN. He means in body.
IRAS. No, he means you'll have to paint when you're old.
CHARMIAN. Heaven forbid wrinkles!
ALEXAS. Don't disturb his foresight. Pay attention.
CHARMIAN. Hush!
SOOTHSAYER. You'll love more than you're loved.
CHARMIAN. I'd rather heat up my liver with drinking.
ALEXAS. No, hear him out.

CHARMIAN. Right then — some excellent fortune! Let me marry three kings in one morning and widow them all. Let me have a child at fifty, to whom Herod of Jewry must pay homage. Arrange for me to marry Octavius Caesar, and make me equal to my mistress.
SOOTHSAYER. You'll outlive the lady you serve.
CHARMIAN. Oh, excellent! I love long life better than figs.
SOOTHSAYER. You've seen and experienced a better fortune in the past than the one to come.
CHARMIAN. Then I suppose my children will have no names. Tell me, how many boys and girls am I going to have?
SOOTHSAYER. If every one of your wishes had a womb, and every wish were fertile — a million.
CHARMIAN. Get out, fool! I'll forgive you because you're a witch.
ALEXAS. You think only your sheets know your wishes.
CHARMIAN. No, come, tell Iras hers.
ALEXAS. We'll know all our fortunes.
ENOBARBUS. My fortune, and most of ours tonight, will be to drink ourselves to bed.
IRAS. There's a palm that promises chastity, if nothing else.
CHARMIAN. Just like the overflowing Nile promises famine.
IRAS. Off with you, you wild bedmate, you can't tell fortunes.
CHARMIAN. No, if a moist palm isn't a sign of fertility, I can't scratch my ear. Please, just tell her a workaday fortune.
SOOTHSAYER. Your fortunes are alike.
IRAS. But how, but how? Give me details.
SOOTHSAYER. I've spoken.
IRAS. Am I not even an inch of fortune better than she is?
CHARMIAN. Well, if you were just an inch of fortune better than me, where would you place it?
IRAS. Not in my husband's nose.

CHARMIAN. May the heavens fix our worse thoughts! Alexas — come, his fortune! his fortune! Oh, let him marry a woman who can't walk, sweet Isis, I beg you, and let her die too, and give him a worse one, and let worse follow worse, until the worst of all follows him laughing to his grave, a fifty-times cuckold! Good Isis, hear me this prayer, even if you deny me something more important; good Isis, I beg you!

IRAS. Amen. Dear goddess, hear that prayer of the people! For just as it's heartbreaking to see a handsome man unfaithfully married, so it's a deadly sorrow to see a vile knave who hasn't been cuckolded. Therefore, dear Isis, keep decorum and grant him his fortune accordingly!
CHARMIAN. Amen.
ALEXAS. Look at that — if it were in their power to make me a cuckold, they'd turn themselves into whores just to do it!
[Enter CLEOPATRA.]
ENOBARBUS. Hush, here comes Antony.
CHARMIAN. Not him — the queen.
CLEOPATRA. Did you see my lord?
ENOBARBUS. No, my lady.
CLEOPATRA. Wasn't he here?
CHARMIAN. No, madam.
CLEOPATRA. He was in a mood for laughter; but suddenly a Roman thought has struck him. Enobarbus!
ENOBARBUS. Madam?
CLEOPATRA. Seek him out and bring him here. Where's Alexas?
ALEXAS. Here, at your service. My lord approaches.
[Enter ANTONY with a Messenger.]
CLEOPATRA. We won't look at him. Come with us.
[Exeunt CLEOPATRA, ENOBARBUS, CHARMIAN, IRAS, ALEXAS and Soothsayer.]
MESSENGER. Fulvia, your wife, first took the field.
ANTONY. Against my brother Lucius.
MESSENGER. Yes. But that war soon ended, and the situation made friends of them, joining their forces against Caesar, whose better luck in the war from Italy drove them out at the first encounter.
ANTONY. Well, what's the worst?
MESSENGER. The nature of bad news infects the messenger who brings it.
ANTONY. Only when it concerns the fool or coward. Go on. What's past is finished for me. It's this: whoever tells me the truth, even if his story carries death, I hear him out as if he flattered me.
MESSENGER. Labienus — this is harsh news — has, with his Parthian force, extended Asia from the Euphrates; his conquering banner has waved from Syria to Lydia and to Ionia, while —
ANTONY. "Antony," you mean to say —
MESSENGER. Oh, my lord!

ANTONY. Speak plainly to me; don't soften the common phrase. Name Cleopatra as she's called in Rome; rail in Fulvia's manner, and mock my faults with all the freedom that both truth and malice have the power to express. Oh, then we grow weeds when our quick minds lie still, and our faults told to us are like our plowing. Farewell for a while.
MESSENGER. At your noble pleasure.
[Exit Messenger.]
[Enter another Messenger.]
ANTONY. From Sicyon, hey, what's the news? Speak there!
SECOND MESSENGER. The man from Sicyon —
ANTONY. Is there such a one?
SECOND MESSENGER. He waits on your pleasure.
ANTONY. Let him appear.
[Exit second Messenger.]
These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, or lose myself in infatuation.
[Enter another Messenger with a letter.]
Who are you?
THIRD MESSENGER. Fulvia, your wife, is dead.
ANTONY. Where did she die?
THIRD MESSENGER. In Sicyon. The length of her illness, along with whatever else more serious it's important for you to know, this letter carries.
[Gives a letter.]
ANTONY. Leave me.
[Exit third Messenger.]

A great spirit is gone! This is what I desired. What our contempt often throws away, we wish back again. The present pleasure, sinking through revolution, becomes its own opposite. She's good, now she's gone. The hand that shoved her on could pluck her back. I must break off from this enchanting queen. Ten thousand troubles, worse than the ones I know, are hatched by my idleness. Well now, Enobarbus!
[Enter ENOBARBUS.]
ENOBARBUS. What's your pleasure, sir?
ANTONY. I must leave here quickly.
ENOBARBUS. Why then, we kill all our women. We see how deadly an unkindness is to them. If they have to endure our departure, death's the word.
ANTONY. I must be gone.

ENOBARBUS. When there's a compelling reason, let women die. It would be a shame to cast them off for nothing — though, set against a great cause, they ought to be counted as nothing. Cleopatra, catching the faintest whisper of this, will die instantly. I've seen her die twenty times on far slighter occasions. I think there must be some quality in death that performs a loving act on her, she has such a quickness in dying.
ANTONY. She's craftier than any man can imagine.

ENOBARBUS. Alas, sir, no; her passions are made of nothing but the finest part of pure love. We cannot call her winds and waters sighs and tears; they're greater storms and tempests than almanacs can report. This can't be cunning in her; if it is, she can make a shower of rain as well as Jove does.
ANTONY. I wish I'd never seen her!
ENOBARBUS. Oh, sir, then you'd have left unseen a wonderful piece of work, and not to have been blessed with the sight would have discredited your travels.
ANTONY. Fulvia is dead.
ENOBARBUS. Sir?
ANTONY. Fulvia is dead.
ENOBARBUS. Fulvia?
ANTONY. Dead.

ENOBARBUS. Why, sir, give the gods a thankful sacrifice. When it pleases their deities to take a man's wife from him, it shows the man earth's tailors; comforting him with the thought that when old robes are worn out, there are people to make new ones. If there were no more women but Fulvia, then you'd have indeed taken a hit, and the case would be worth lamenting. This grief is crowned with consolation; your old smock brings forth a new petticoat — and really, the tears that should water this sorrow live in an onion.
ANTONY. The business she's started in the state cannot endure my absence.
ENOBARBUS. And the business you've started here can't survive without you — especially Cleopatra's, which depends entirely on your staying.

ANTONY. No more flippant answers. Let our officers know what we intend. I'll explain the reason for our urgency to the queen, and get her permission to leave. For not only does the death of Fulvia, with more pressing matters, speak strongly to us, but the letters too from many of our scheming friends in Rome petition us to come home. Sextus Pompeius has openly defied Caesar, and commands the empire of the sea. Our fickle people, whose love is never attached to the deserving man until his deserts are past, begin to throw Pompey the Great's name and dignities onto his son, who, high in name and power — higher than both in blood and spirit — stands forth as the chief soldier; whose strength, if it grows, may put the sides of the world in danger. Much is brewing which, like horsehair in water, has life but not yet a serpent's poison. Tell those subordinate to us that our pleasure requires our quick departure from here.
ENOBARBUS. I'll see to it.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Alexandria. A Room in Cleopatra’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, Alexas and IRAS.]
CLEOPATRA. Where is he?
CHARMIAN. I haven't seen him since.
CLEOPATRA. Find out where he is, who's with him, what he's doing. I didn't send you. If you find him sad, say I'm dancing; if cheerful, report that I've suddenly fallen ill. Quick, and come back.
[Exit Alexas.]
CHARMIAN. Madam, I think, if you truly loved him, you're not using the right method to draw the same love from him.
CLEOPATRA. What should I be doing that I'm not?
CHARMIAN. In everything give him his way; cross him in nothing.
CLEOPATRA. You're teaching like a fool — that's the way to lose him.
CHARMIAN. Don't push him so far; I beg you, restrain yourself. In time we hate what we often fear. But here comes Antony.
[Enter ANTONY.]
CLEOPATRA. I am sick and sullen.
ANTONY. I'm sorry to put words to my purpose —
CLEOPATRA. Help me away, dear Charmian! I'm going to fall. This can't last; nature's sides won't bear it.
ANTONY. Now, my dearest queen —
CLEOPATRA. Please, stand farther away from me.
ANTONY. What's the matter?

CLEOPATRA. I can tell by that same look in your eye there's some good news. What — does your wife say you may go? I wish she'd never given you leave to come! Don't let her say it's me keeping you here. I have no power over you; you're hers.
ANTONY. The gods know best —
CLEOPATRA. Oh, never was there a queen so mightily betrayed! Yet from the very first I saw the treasons planted.
ANTONY. Cleopatra —

CLEOPATRA. Why should I think you can be mine and true — though in swearing you make the enthroned gods shake — when you've been false to Fulvia? Reckless madness, to be entangled with those vows made of mouth alone, which break themselves in the swearing!
ANTONY. Sweetest queen —

CLEOPATRA. No, please don't dress up an excuse for your going; just say goodbye and go. When you were begging to stay, that was the time for words. No talk of leaving then — eternity was in our lips and eyes, bliss in the curve of our brows; no part of ourselves was so trivial that it wasn't a race from heaven. They still are, or else you, the greatest soldier in the world, have turned the greatest liar.
ANTONY. What's this, lady!
CLEOPATRA. I wish I had your height and strength — you'd know there's a heart in Egypt.

ANTONY. Hear me, queen: the strong necessity of the moment commands our services for a while, but my full heart remains in use with you. Our Italy gleams with civil swords; Sextus Pompeius approaches the port of Rome; equality of two domestic powers breeds quarrelsome faction; the hated, now grown strong, have newly grown into favor; the condemned Pompey, rich in his father's honor, creeps quickly into the hearts of those who haven't prospered under the present regime, and their numbers are a threat; quietness, grown sick of rest, would purge itself by any desperate change. My more personal reason — and the one that should most reassure you about my going — is Fulvia's death.
CLEOPATRA. Though age couldn't free me from folly, it does free me from childishness. Can Fulvia die?
ANTONY. She's dead, my queen. Look here, and at your sovereign leisure read the disturbances she stirred up; at the last, best, see when and where she died.
CLEOPATRA. Oh, most false love! Where are the sacred vials you should fill with sorrowful water? Now I see, I see, in Fulvia's death how mine will be received.

ANTONY. Quarrel no more, but be prepared to know the purposes I carry; which will go forward, or stop, as you advise. By the fire that quickens the Nile's slime, I leave here as your soldier, your servant, making peace or war as you wish.
CLEOPATRA. Cut my lace, Charmian, come! No, let it be; I'm quickly ill and well, as Antony loves me.
ANTONY. My precious queen, restrain yourself, and give true evidence to his love, which stands an honorable trial.

CLEOPATRA. So Fulvia told me. Please, turn aside and weep for her, then say goodbye to me, and say the tears belong to Egypt. Come now, play one scene of excellent pretending, and let it look like perfect honor.
ANTONY. You'll heat my blood. No more.
CLEOPATRA. You can do better yet, but this is acceptable.
ANTONY. Now, by my sword —
CLEOPATRA. And shield. Still he gets better. But this isn't his best. Look, please, Charmian, how well this Herculean Roman carries off his fit of temper.
ANTONY. I'll leave you, lady.

CLEOPATRA. Courteous lord, one word. Sir, you and I must part — but that's not it; sir, you and I have loved — but there's not it either; you know that well enough. There's something I wanted to — oh, my forgetfulness is itself a perfect Antony, and I've forgotten everything.
ANTONY. If your royalty didn't keep idleness as its subject, I'd take you for idleness itself.

CLEOPATRA. It's sweating labor to carry such idleness so close to the heart as Cleopatra does. But, sir, forgive me, since my graces kill me when they don't look well to you. Your honor calls you away; therefore be deaf to my unpitied folly, and all the gods go with you! May laurel victory sit on your sword, and smooth success be strewn before your feet!
ANTONY. Let us go. Come. Our separation so stays and flies that you, residing here, still go with me, and I, leaving here, remain with you. Away!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — Rome. An Apartment in Caesar’s House
paragraphs: [Enter Octavius CAESAR, LEPIDUS and their train.]

CAESAR. You can see, Lepidus, and may know from now on, that it isn't Caesar's natural vice to hate our great rival. From Alexandria comes this news: he fishes, drinks, and wastes the night's lamps in revelry; he's no more manly than Cleopatra, nor is Ptolemy's queen more womanly than he; he scarcely granted audience, nor even bothered to consider that he has partners. You'll find there a man who is the very abstract of every fault that all men follow.

LEPIDUS. I can't believe there are enough vices to darken all his virtues. His faults in him seem like the spots of heaven, more fiery against night's blackness; inherited rather than acquired — things he cannot change rather than things he chooses.

CAESAR. You're too indulgent. Let's grant that it isn't wrong to tumble on Ptolemy's bed, to trade a kingdom for a laugh, to sit and take turns drinking with a slave, to stagger through the streets at noon, and trade blows with knaves who smell of sweat. Say this suits him — for his composure must indeed be rare whom such things can't tarnish — yet Antony has no excuse for his failures when we have to bear such great weight in consequence of his flippancy. If he were filling his idle hours with his own debauchery, full surfeits and the dryness of his bones would call him to account for it. But to squander such time as drums him from his pleasure, and speaks as loudly as both his own welfare and ours, deserves to be scolded as we scold boys who, being mature in knowledge, pawn their experience for present pleasure and so rebel against judgment.
[Enter a Messenger.]
LEPIDUS. Here's more news.

MESSENGER. Your orders have been carried out, and every hour, most noble Caesar, you shall have a report on how things stand abroad. Pompey is strong at sea, and it seems he's loved by those who only ever feared Caesar. The malcontents flock to the ports, and people say he has been much wronged.

CAESAR. I should have expected no less. We've been taught from the earliest age that the man in power was wished for until he was in power, and the man who's lost favor — never loved until he's no longer worth loving — becomes treasured by being missed. This common crowd, like a wandering flag on the current, drifts to and fro, attending the changing tide, until it rots itself with motion.
[Enter a second Messenger.]

SECOND MESSENGER. Caesar, I bring you word that Menecrates and Menas, notorious pirates, make the sea serve them, plowing and wounding it with keels of every kind. They make many fierce raids into Italy — the maritime borders go pale at the thought of it — and our hot-blooded youth defect. No vessel can peek out without being captured as soon as seen, for Pompey's name strikes more terror than his war, if resisted, could.

CAESAR. Antony, leave your lecherous carousing. When you were once driven from Modena, where you killed the consuls Hirtius and Pansa, famine followed at your heel; you fought against famine, though delicately raised, with more patience than savages could endure. You drank the urine of horses and the slime-coated puddle that beasts would gag at. Your palate then condescended to the roughest berry on the meanest hedge. Yes, like a stag when snow blankets the pasture, you browsed on the bark of trees. On the Alps, it's reported, you ate strange flesh that some died from merely looking at. And all this — it wounds your honor that I mention it now — was borne so soldierly that your cheek didn't even thin.
LEPIDUS. It's a pity for him.
CAESAR. Let his shame quickly drive him to Rome. It's time we two showed ourselves in the field, and to that end let's assemble a council at once. Pompey thrives on our idleness.
LEPIDUS. Tomorrow, Caesar, I'll be ready to inform you accurately of what, by sea and by land, I can muster to confront the present situation.
CAESAR. Until that meeting, that's my business too. Farewell.
LEPIDUS. Farewell, my lord. Whatever you learn meanwhile of stirrings abroad, I'd ask you, sir, to let me share in it.
CAESAR. Don't doubt it, sir. I knew that was my obligation.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS and Mardian.]
CLEOPATRA. Charmian!
CHARMIAN. Madam?
CLEOPATRA. Ha, ha! Give me some mandrake to drink.
CHARMIAN. Why, madam?
CLEOPATRA. So I might sleep through this great gap of time my Antony is away.
CHARMIAN. You think of him too much.
CLEOPATRA. Oh, that's treason!
CHARMIAN. Madam, I trust it isn't.
CLEOPATRA. You, eunuch Mardian!
MARDIAN. What is your highness's pleasure?
CLEOPATRA. Not now to hear you sing. I take no pleasure in anything a eunuch has. It's well for you that, being unmanned, your freer thoughts can't fly out of Egypt. Do you have desires?
MARDIAN. Yes, gracious madam.
CLEOPATRA. Really?
MARDIAN. Not in deed, madam, for I can do nothing but what is honestly possible. Yet I have fierce desires, and think on what Venus did with Mars.

CLEOPATRA. Oh, Charmian, where do you think he is now? Is he standing, or sitting? Or is he walking? Or is he on his horse? Oh, happy horse, to bear the weight of Antony! Do bravely, horse — do you know whom you carry? The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm and helmet of men. He's speaking now, or murmuring, "Where's my serpent of old Nile?" For so he calls me. Now I feed myself with most delicious poison. Think on me, who am blackened by Phoebus's amorous pinches, and deeply wrinkled by time? Broad-browed Caesar, when you were here above the ground, I was a morsel fit for a monarch. And great Pompey would stand and let his eyes grow into my brow; there he would anchor his gaze, and die looking at his life.
[Enter Alexas.]
ALEXAS. Sovereign of Egypt, hail!
CLEOPATRA. How unlike Mark Antony you are! Yet, coming from him, that great elixir has gilded you with his tincture. How is my brave Mark Antony?
ALEXAS. The last thing he did, dear queen, was kiss — the last of many doubled kisses — this oriental pearl. His speech sticks in my heart.
CLEOPATRA. My ear must pluck it from there.

ALEXAS. "Good friend," he said, "say that the firm Roman sends to great Egypt this treasure from an oyster; at whose foot, to make up for the petty gift, I will add to her opulent throne with whole kingdoms. All the east," he said, "shall call her mistress." Then he nodded, and gravely mounted a lean-armed steed, which neighed so loudly that whatever I might have said was beastly silenced by him.
CLEOPATRA. What, was he sad or merry?
ALEXAS. Like the season of the year between the extremes of hot and cold, he was neither sad nor merry.

CLEOPATRA. Oh, well-balanced disposition! — Note him, note him, good Charmian, that's the man — but note him: he was not sad, for he wanted to shine upon those who take their cue from his look; he was not merry, which seemed to tell them his memory lay in Egypt with his joy; but between both. Oh, heavenly mixture! — Whether you're sad or merry, the violence of either suits you, as it does no man else. — Did you meet my messengers?
ALEXAS. Yes, madam, twenty different messengers. Why do you send so many?
CLEOPATRA. Whoever's born the day I forget to send to Antony shall die a beggar. — Ink and paper, Charmian. — Welcome, my good Alexas. — Did I, Charmian, ever love Caesar this much?
CHARMIAN. Oh, that brave Caesar!
CLEOPATRA. May you choke on another such phrase! Say "the brave Antony."
CHARMIAN. The valiant Caesar!
CLEOPATRA. By Isis, I'll give you bloody teeth if you compare Caesar with my man of men again.
CHARMIAN. By your most gracious pardon, I'm only singing what you taught me.

CLEOPATRA. My salad days, when I was green in judgment, cold in blood, to talk as I did then. But come, away — get me ink and paper. He shall have a different greeting every day, or I'll empty Egypt of people.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Messina. A Room in Pompey’s house
paragraphs: [Enter POMPEY, MENECRATES and MENAS in warlike manner.]
POMPEY. If the great gods are just, they will assist the deeds of the most just men.
MENECRATES. Know, worthy Pompey, that what they delay they don't deny.
POMPEY. While we are petitioners at their throne, the very thing we sue for decays.
MENECRATES. We, being ignorant of ourselves, often beg for our own harms, which the wise powers deny us for our own good — so we find profit by losing our prayers.

POMPEY. I shall do well. The people love me, and the sea is mine. My forces are growing, and my prophetic hope says they will come to the full. Mark Antony sits at dinner in Egypt and will not make wars outside its doors. Caesar gets money where he loses hearts. Lepidus flatters both, and is flattered by both, but he neither loves either nor either cares for him.
MENAS. Caesar and Lepidus are in the field. They carry a mighty strength.
POMPEY. Where did you hear this? It's false.
MENAS. From Silvius, sir.

POMPEY. He dreams. I know they are in Rome together, looking for Antony. But all the charms of love, salt Cleopatra, soften your faded lip! Let witchcraft join with beauty, lust with both. Tie up the libertine in a field of feasts; keep his brain fuming. Let Epicurean cooks sharpen his appetite with sauces that never satisfy, so that sleep and feeding may suspend his honor even until a forgetful dullness—
[Enter VARRIUS.]
How now, Varrius!
VARRIUS. This is most certain news I bring: Mark Antony is expected in Rome any hour now. Since he left Egypt, there's been time for a longer journey.

POMPEY. I would have given lesser news a better hearing. — Menas, I didn't think this amorous indulger would put on his helmet for such a petty war. His soldiership is twice that of the other two. But let us raise our opinion of ourselves higher, since our stirring can pluck the never-lust-wearied Antony from the lap of Egypt's widow.
MENAS. I can't hope Caesar and Antony will greet each other well. Antony's dead wife committed offenses against Caesar; his brother made war on him, though I don't think Antony moved him to it.

POMPEY. I don't know, Menas, how lesser enmities may give way to greater ones. If we weren't standing up against them all, it's likely they would quarrel among themselves, since they have plenty of cause to draw their swords. But how the fear of us may cement their divisions and patch up petty differences, we don't yet know. Let it be as our gods will have it! It only depends on our lives that we use our strongest hands. Come, Menas.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Rome. A Room in the House of Lepidus
paragraphs: [Enter ENOBARBUS and LEPIDUS.]
LEPIDUS. Good Enobarbus, it's a worthy deed and will suit you well to ask your captain to speak softly and gently.

ENOBARBUS. I'll ask him to answer as himself. If Caesar provokes him, let Antony look over Caesar's head and speak as loudly as Mars. By Jupiter, if I were the wearer of Antony's beard, I would not shave it today.
LEPIDUS. This isn't a time for private grudges.
ENOBARBUS. Every time serves for whatever matter is born in it.
LEPIDUS. But small matters must give way to greater.
ENOBARBUS. Not if the small ones come first.
LEPIDUS. Your speech is passion. But please, don't stir up any embers. Here comes the noble Antony.
[Enter ANTONY and VENTIDIUS.]
ENOBARBUS. And over there, Caesar.
[Enter CAESAR, MAECENAS and AGRIPPA.]
ANTONY. If we settle things well here, on to Parthia. Listen, Ventidius.
CAESAR. I don't know, Maecenas. Ask Agrippa.

LEPIDUS. Noble friends, what brought us together was most great — don't let a leaner matter tear us apart. Whatever's amiss, let it be heard gently. When we debate our trivial differences loudly, we commit murder in the act of healing wounds. So, noble partners — I earnestly beg — touch on the sourest points with the sweetest terms, and don't let bitterness grow on the matter.
ANTONY. Well spoken. If we were before our armies and about to fight, I would do exactly this.
CAESAR. Welcome to Rome.
ANTONY. Thank you.
CAESAR. Sit.
ANTONY. You sit, sir.
CAESAR. Well, then.
ANTONY. I hear you take offense at things that aren't offensive, or if they are, don't concern you.

CAESAR. I would be laughed at if I claimed to be offended over nothing or trifles — and at you in particular, the chief man in the world. More laughed at still if I should ever mention your name disparagingly when speaking your name had nothing to do with me.
ANTONY. My being in Egypt, Caesar — what was that to you?
CAESAR. No more than my staying here in Rome might be to you in Egypt. Yet if while there you plotted against my state, your being in Egypt would be my concern.
ANTONY. What do you mean, plotted?
CAESAR. You may try to grasp my meaning from what happened to me here. Your wife and brother made war on me, and their quarrel concerned you — you were the watchword of their war.

ANTONY. You mistake the business. My brother never invoked me in his action. I have inquired, and have my information from some truthful reports — from men who drew their swords with you. Didn't he rather discredit my authority along with yours, and wage the war just as much against my own interest, since your cause was mine too? My earlier letters satisfied you on this. If you want to patch up a quarrel — when you don't have a whole matter to make one out of — it must not be with this.
CAESAR. You praise yourself by laying defects of judgment at my feet — but you patched together your excuses.

ANTONY. Not so, not so. I'm certain you couldn't lack — couldn't fail to think — that I, your partner in the cause he fought against, couldn't look with gracious eyes on those wars that opposed my own peace. As for my wife, I wish you had her spirit in such another. A third of the world is yours, and you can pace it easily with a snaffle — but not such a wife.
ENOBARBUS. I wish we all had such wives, so the men might go to war alongside the women.

ANTONY. So uncurbable, Caesar — the disorders made from her impatience, which had its share of shrewd policy too — I grieve to admit gave you too much disquiet. For that, you must just say I couldn't help it.
CAESAR. I wrote to you when you were rioting in Alexandria. You pocketed up my letters, and with taunts jeered my messenger out of audience.

ANTONY. Sir, he forced himself on me before being admitted, then. I had just feasted three kings and was lacking the composure I had had in the morning. But the next day I explained myself to him, which was as good as asking his pardon. Let this fellow be no part of our strife. If we are to argue, leave him out of the question.
CAESAR. You've broken the article of your oath, which you'll never have a tongue to charge me with.
LEPIDUS. Softly, Caesar!
ANTONY. No, Lepidus, let him speak. The honor he speaks of is sacred, supposing I lacked it. But go on, Caesar — the article of my oath?
CAESAR. To lend me arms and aid when I needed them, both of which you denied.

ANTONY. Neglected, rather. And then when poisoned hours had bound me up from my own knowledge. As best as I can, I'll play the penitent to you. But my honesty won't impoverish my greatness, nor my power work without it. The truth is that Fulvia, to get me out of Egypt, made wars here. For that, I — the ignorant cause — ask pardon as far as my honor can stoop in such a case.
LEPIDUS. Nobly spoken.
MAECENAS. May it please you not to press the grievances between you any further. To forget them entirely would be to remember that the present need urges you to reconcile.
LEPIDUS. Worthily said, Maecenas.
ENOBARBUS. Or, if you borrow each other's love for the moment, when you no longer hear any news of Pompey, you can give it back. You'll have time to quarrel when you've nothing else to do.
ANTONY. You're only a soldier. Speak no more.
ENOBARBUS. I'd almost forgotten that truth should be silent.
ANTONY. You wrong this company. So speak no more.
ENOBARBUS. All right, then. Your discreet stone!

CAESAR. I don't mind the substance of what he said so much as the manner of it — for we can't remain in friendship if our temperaments differ so much in action. Yet if I knew what hoop would hold us together firmly, from edge to edge of the world I would pursue it.
AGRIPPA. Allow me, Caesar.
CAESAR. Speak, Agrippa.
AGRIPPA. You have a sister on your mother's side, the admired Octavia. The great Mark Antony is now a widower.
CAESAR. Don't say so, Agrippa. If Cleopatra heard you, you'd well deserve a rebuke for rashness.
ANTONY. I am not married, Caesar. Let me hear Agrippa speak further.

AGRIPPA. To hold you both in perpetual amity, to make you brothers, and to knit your hearts with an unslipping knot, give Antony Octavia as his wife. Her beauty claims no worse a husband than the best of men; her virtue and her general graces speak what no one else can express. By this marriage, all the small jealousies that now seem great, and all the great fears that now bring their dangers, would become nothing. Truths would be reduced to mere tales, where now half-truths pass as truth. Her love for both of you would draw each to the other, and all loves to both. Pardon what I've spoken — it's a studied thought, not a present one, ruminated by duty.
ANTONY. Will Caesar speak?
CAESAR. Not until he hears how Antony is moved by what's already been said.
ANTONY. What power does Agrippa have, if I should say "Agrippa, let it be so," to make this good?
CAESAR. The power of Caesar, and his power over Octavia.

ANTONY. May I never, in the way of this good purpose that shows so fairly, dream of any impediment! Let me have your hand. Further this act of grace, and from this hour let the heart of brothers govern in our loves and direct our great designs!
CAESAR. Here's my hand. I bequeath you a sister whom no brother has ever loved so dearly. Let her live to join our kingdoms and our hearts, and never let our loves fly apart again!
LEPIDUS. Happily — amen!
ANTONY. I didn't expect to draw my sword against Pompey, for he has done me strange and great courtesies of late. I must thank him first, lest my remembrance suffer ill report. After that, defy him.
LEPIDUS. Time calls on us. We must seek Pompey out promptly, or else he'll seek us out.
ANTONY. Where is he?
CAESAR. About Mount Misenum.
ANTONY. What's his strength on land?
CAESAR. Great and increasing. But by sea he is absolute master.
ANTONY. So fame reports. I wish we had spoken together! Let's hasten to it. But before we take up arms, let's dispatch the business we've been discussing.
CAESAR. With the greatest gladness. I invite you to meet my sister, where I'll lead you straightaway.
ANTONY. Lepidus, don't let us go without your company.
LEPIDUS. Noble Antony, not even sickness would detain me.
[Flourish. Exeunt all except ENOBARBUS, AGRIPPA and MAECENAS.]
MAECENAS. Welcome back from Egypt, sir.
ENOBARBUS. Half the heart of Caesar, worthy Maecenas! My honorable friend, Agrippa!
AGRIPPA. Good Enobarbus!
MAECENAS. We have reason to be glad that matters have been so well digested. You stayed put in Egypt.
ENOBARBUS. Yes, sir, we slept the day out of countenance and made the night bright with drinking.
MAECENAS. Eight wild boars roasted whole at a single breakfast, and only twelve persons present. Is this true?
ENOBARBUS. That was just a fly compared to an eagle. We had much more monstrous feasts that worthily deserved noting.
MAECENAS. She's a most triumphant lady, if reports do her justice.
ENOBARBUS. When she first met Mark Antony, she pocketed up his heart on the river of Cydnus.
AGRIPPA. There she appeared indeed — or my source invented well for her.

ENOBARBUS. I'll tell you. The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne, burned on the water. The poop was beaten gold; the sails were purple, and so perfumed that the winds were love-sick with them. The oars were silver, which kept stroke to the tune of flutes, and made the water they beat follow faster, as if enamored of their strokes. As for her own person, it beggared all description: she lay in her pavilion, cloth-of-gold of tissue, outdoing that picture of Venus where we see the imagination outwork nature. On each side of her stood pretty dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids, with many-colored fans, whose wind seemed to glow the delicate cheeks they cooled — and what they undid, did.
AGRIPPA. Oh, rare for Antony!

ENOBARBUS. Her gentlewomen, like the Nereids — so many mermaids — attended her with their eyes, and made their bows ornaments. At the helm a seeming mermaid steers. The silken rigging swells under the touches of those flower-soft hands that briskly handle the office. From the barge a strange invisible perfume strikes the senses on the nearby wharves. The city cast its people out upon her, and Antony, enthroned in the market-place, sat alone, whistling to the air — which, but for the vacuum it would have left, would have gone to gaze on Cleopatra too, and made a gap in nature.
AGRIPPA. Rare Egyptian!

ENOBARBUS. When she landed, Antony sent for her, inviting her to supper. She replied it would be better if he became her guest, which she requested. Our courteous Antony — whom no woman ever heard say the word "No" — being barbered ten times over, goes to the feast, and for his meal pays his heart for what his eyes only ate.
AGRIPPA. Royal wench! She made great Caesar lay his sword to bed. He ploughed her, and she yielded a crop.

ENOBARBUS. I once saw her hop forty paces through a public street, and having lost her breath, she spoke and panted in such a way that she made defect into perfection, and, breathless, poured breath forth.
MAECENAS. Now Antony must leave her completely.

ENOBARBUS. Never. He won't. Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale her infinite variety. Other women cloy the appetites they feed, but she makes hungry where she most satisfies. For the vilest things become becoming in her, so that the holy priests bless her when she is wanton.
MAECENAS. If beauty, wisdom, and modesty can settle the heart of Antony, Octavia is a blessed lottery for him.
AGRIPPA. Let's go. Good Enobarbus, make yourself my guest while you stay here.
ENOBARBUS. Humbly, sir, I thank you.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — Rome. A Room in Caesar’s House
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY, CAESAR, OCTAVIA between them.]
ANTONY. The world and my great office will sometimes divide me from your embrace.
OCTAVIA. All that time, my knee shall bow my prayers before the gods on your behalf.
ANTONY. Good night, sir. — My Octavia, don't read my blemishes in the world's report. I have not kept my square, but what's to come shall all be done by the rule. Good night, dear lady.
OCTAVIA. Good night, sir.
CAESAR. Good night.
[Exeunt CAESAR and OCTAVIA.]
[Enter Soothsayer.]
ANTONY. Now, fellow — you wish yourself back in Egypt?
SOOTHSAYER. I wish I had never come from there, nor you gone there!
ANTONY. If you can, your reason.
SOOTHSAYER. I see it in my intuition, but can't speak it on my tongue. Still, hurry back to Egypt.
ANTONY. Tell me — whose fortunes will rise higher, Caesar's or mine?

SOOTHSAYER. Caesar's. Therefore, O Antony, don't stay near him. Your guardian spirit — the daemon that keeps you — is noble, courageous, high, unmatchable, where Caesar's is not. But near him, your angel becomes afraid, as if overpowered. So make space enough between you.
ANTONY. Speak no more of this.

SOOTHSAYER. To no one but you, and no more than when speaking with you. If you play any game with him, you're sure to lose. And by that natural luck of his, he beats you against the odds. Your luster dims when he shines beside you. I say again, your spirit is afraid to govern you near him — but with him away, it's noble.
ANTONY. Be gone. Tell Ventidius I want to speak with him.
[Exit Soothsayer.]

He shall go to Parthia. Whether by skill or chance, he has spoken true. The very dice obey him, and in our games my better cunning falters against his luck. If we draw lots, he wins. His fighting cocks always beat mine when it's all-or-nothing, and his quails always beat mine — penned in the ring, against the odds. I'll go to Egypt. And though I make this marriage for my peace, my pleasure lies in the East.
[Enter VENTIDIUS.]
Oh, come, Ventidius, you must go to Parthia. Your commission is ready. Follow me and receive it.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Rome. A street
paragraphs: [Enter LEPIDUS, MAECENAS and AGRIPPA.]
LEPIDUS. Don't trouble yourselves any further. Please send your generals on after.
AGRIPPA. Sir, Mark Antony will just kiss Octavia goodbye, and we'll follow.
LEPIDUS. Farewell until I see you in your soldier's dress, which will suit you both.
MAECENAS. As I figure the journey, we shall be at the Mount before you, Lepidus.
LEPIDUS. Your route is shorter. My business pulls me around much further. You'll gain two days on me.
BOTH. Sir, good success!
LEPIDUS. Farewell.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 5 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, ALEXAS.]
CLEOPATRA. Give me some music — music, the moody food of those of us who trade in love.
ALL. The music, ho!
[Enter MARDIAN, the eunuch.]
CLEOPATRA. Leave it. Let's play billiards. Come, Charmian.
CHARMIAN. My arm is sore. You'd better play with Mardian.
CLEOPATRA. A woman might as well play with a eunuch as with a woman. Come, will you play with me, sir?
MARDIAN. As well as I can, madam.

CLEOPATRA. And when good will is shown, even if it falls short, the actor may plead pardon. I don't want to play now. Give me my fishing rod — we'll go to the river. There, with my music playing far off, I will betray tawny-finned fish. My bent hook shall pierce their slimy jaws, and as I draw them up I'll think each one an Antony, and say, "Ah, ha! You're caught."
CHARMIAN. It was merry when you wagered on your fishing — when your diver hung a salt fish on your hook, which you eagerly drew up.

CLEOPATRA. That time? — Oh, those times! — I laughed him out of patience; and that night I laughed him into patience; and the next morning, before the ninth hour, I drank him to his bed, then put my dresses and mantles on him, while I wore his sword Philippan.
[Enter Messenger.]
Oh! From Italy! Ram your fruitful tidings into my ears, which have been barren for so long.
MESSENGER. Madam, madam—

CLEOPATRA. Antony's dead! If you say so, villain, you kill your mistress. But if you say he's well and free, there's gold for you, and here my bluest veins to kiss — a hand that kings have kissed, trembling.
MESSENGER. First, madam, he's well.
CLEOPATRA. Why, there's more gold. But mark this, fellow — we say the dead are well. If you bring it to that, the gold I give you I'll melt and pour down your ill-speaking throat.
MESSENGER. Good madam, hear me.

CLEOPATRA. Well, go on, I will. But there's no goodness in your face — not if Antony is free and healthy. Such a sour expression to trumpet such good news! If not well, you should come like a Fury crowned with snakes, not like an ordinary man.
MESSENGER. Will it please you to hear me?

CLEOPATRA. I have a mind to strike you before you speak. Yet if you say Antony lives, is well, friends with Caesar, and not his captive, I'll set you in a shower of gold and hail rich pearls upon you.
MESSENGER. Madam, he's well.
CLEOPATRA. Well said.
MESSENGER. And friends with Caesar.
CLEOPATRA. You're an honest man.
MESSENGER. Caesar and he are greater friends than ever.
CLEOPATRA. I'll make your fortune.
MESSENGER. But yet, madam—

CLEOPATRA. I don't like "But yet" — it taints the good that came before. Shame on "But yet"! "But yet" is like a jailer bringing forth some monstrous criminal. Please, friend, pour out the whole pack of your news into my ear, the good and bad together: he's friends with Caesar, in good health, you say — and free, you say.
MESSENGER. Free, madam? No. I made no such report. He's bound to Octavia.
CLEOPATRA. For what good purpose?
MESSENGER. For the best purpose in the bed.
CLEOPATRA. I'm pale, Charmian.
MESSENGER. Madam, he's married to Octavia.
CLEOPATRA. The most infectious plague upon you!
[Strikes him down.]
MESSENGER. Good madam, patience.
CLEOPATRA. What do you say?
[Strikes him again.]
Out, horrible villain, or I'll kick your eyes like balls before me! I'll pull the hair from your head!
[She drags him up and down.]
You shall be whipped with wire and stewed in brine, smarting in lingering pickle.
MESSENGER. Gracious madam, I who bring the news did not make the match.

CLEOPATRA. Say it isn't so, and I'll give you a province, and make your fortunes great. The blow I gave you shall be peace-offering for moving me to rage, and I'll reward you with whatever gift besides your modesty can ask.
MESSENGER. He's married, madam.
CLEOPATRA. Rogue, you've lived too long.
[Draws a knife.]
MESSENGER. No, then I'll run. What do you mean, madam? I've done no wrong.
[Exit.]
CHARMIAN. Good madam, keep hold of yourself. The man is innocent.
CLEOPATRA. Some innocents don't escape the thunderbolt. Melt Egypt into the Nile, and let kindly creatures turn all to serpents! Call the slave back. Though I am mad, I won't bite him. Call!
CHARMIAN. He's afraid to come.
CLEOPATRA. I won't hurt him.
[Exit Charmian.]
These hands lack nobility for striking one lower than myself, since I myself have given myself the cause.
[Enter the Messenger again with CHARMIAN.]
Come here, sir. Though it be honest, it is never good to bring bad news. Give to a gracious message a host of tongues, but let bad tidings tell themselves when they are felt.
MESSENGER. I have done my duty.
CLEOPATRA. Is he married? I cannot hate you any worse than I do, if you say "Yes" again.
MESSENGER. He's married, madam.
CLEOPATRA. The gods confound you! Do you still hold to that!
MESSENGER. Should I lie, madam?

CLEOPATRA. Oh, I wish you would — even if half my Egypt were submerged and made a cistern for scaled snakes! Go, get out of here. Even if you had Narcissus's face, you would appear most ugly to me. He is married?
MESSENGER. I crave your highness's pardon.
CLEOPATRA. He is married?
MESSENGER. Don't take offense that I don't want to offend you. To punish me for what you make me do seems very unfair. He's married to Octavia.

CLEOPATRA. Oh, that his fault should make a knave of you, who aren't what you're certain of! Get out of here. The merchandise you've brought from Rome is all too dear for me. Let it stay in your hands, and be ruined by it!
[Exit Messenger.]
CHARMIAN. Good your highness, patience.
CLEOPATRA. In praising Antony I have dispraised Caesar.
CHARMIAN. Many times, madam.

CLEOPATRA. I'm paid for it now. Lead me away from here — I faint. Oh, Iras, Charmian! It doesn't matter. Go to the fellow, good Alexas, and tell him to report the features of Octavia — her age, her disposition; let him not leave out the color of her hair. Bring me word quickly.
[Exit Alexas.]

Let him go forever — no, don't let him go, Charmian. Though painted one way he looks like a Gorgon, the other way he's a Mars. [To Mardian.] Tell Alexas to bring me word how tall she is. Pity me, Charmian, but don't speak to me. Lead me to my chamber.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 6 — Near Misenum
paragraphs: [Flourish. Enter POMPEY and MENAS at one door, with drum and trumpet; at another, CAESAR, LEPIDUS, ANTONY, ENOBARBUS, MAECENAS, AGRIPPA, with Soldiers marching.]
POMPEY. I have your hostages, as you have mine, and we shall talk before we fight.

CAESAR. It's most fitting that we come first to words, and therefore we've sent our written proposals ahead — which, if you've considered them, let us know whether they'll bind up your discontented sword and carry back to Sicily much fine youth that must otherwise perish here.

POMPEY. To you three — the only senators of this great world, chief agents for the gods — I don't know why my father should lack avengers, having a son and friends, since Julius Caesar, who haunted good Brutus at Philippi, saw you laboring for him there. What was it that moved pale Cassius to conspire? And what made the all-honored, honest Roman, Brutus, with his armed companions — courtiers of beautiful freedom — drench the Capitol in blood, but that they wanted to have one man be only a man? And that is what has made me rig my navy — the angered ocean foams under its weight — with which I meant to scourge the ingratitude that spiteful Rome cast upon my noble father.
CAESAR. Take your time.
ANTONY. You cannot frighten us, Pompey, with your sails. We'll deal with you at sea. On land you know how much we outnumber you.
POMPEY. On land indeed you outnumber me with my father's house. But since the cuckoo doesn't build for himself, stay in it as long as you can.
LEPIDUS. Please tell us — leaving that aside for now — how you take the offers we've sent you.
CAESAR. That's the point.
ANTONY. Don't be coaxed into them, but weigh what it's worth to embrace them.
CAESAR. And what may follow if you try a larger fortune.

POMPEY. You've offered me Sicily and Sardinia; in return I must rid all the sea of pirates, and then send measures of wheat to Rome. If this is agreed, we part with unblemished sword-edges and bear our shields back undinted.
CAESAR, ANTONY, and LEPIDUS. That's our offer.

POMPEY. Know, then, that I came here prepared to take this offer. But Mark Antony tried my patience a little. Though I lose credit by mentioning it, you must know that when Caesar and your brother were at blows, your mother came to Sicily and found a friendly welcome.
ANTONY. I have heard it, Pompey, and have studied well to give you the generous thanks I owe you.
POMPEY. Give me your hand. I did not expect to meet you here, sir.
ANTONY. The beds in the East are soft, and thanks to you who called me here sooner than I intended, since I've gained by it.
CAESAR. Since I saw you last, there is a change upon you.
POMPEY. Well, I don't know what harsh marks Fortune casts upon my face, but she shall never enter my heart to make it her vassal.
LEPIDUS. Well met here.
POMPEY. I hope so, Lepidus. So we are agreed. I ask that our agreement be written down and sealed between us.
CAESAR. That's the next thing to do.
POMPEY. We'll feast each other before we part, and let's draw lots for who shall begin.
ANTONY. That I shall do, Pompey.
POMPEY. No, Antony, take the lot. But, first or last, your fine Egyptian cookery shall be most famed. I have heard that Julius Caesar grew fat with feasting there.
ANTONY. You have heard much.
POMPEY. I mean it kindly, sir.
ANTONY. And in kind words.
POMPEY. Then this much I have heard — and I have heard that Apollodorus carried—
ENOBARBUS. No more of that. He did so.
POMPEY. What, please?
ENOBARBUS. A certain queen to Caesar in a mattress.
POMPEY. I know you now. How are you, soldier?
ENOBARBUS. Well — and likely to do well, for I see that four feasts are coming.
POMPEY. Let me shake your hand. I never hated you. I have seen you fight when I envied your conduct.
ENOBARBUS. Sir, I never loved you much, but I have praised you when you well deserved ten times as much praise as I gave.
POMPEY. Enjoy your plainness. It suits you nothing ill. I invite you all aboard my galley. Will you lead the way, lords?
CAESAR, ANTONY, and LEPIDUS. Show us the way, sir.
POMPEY. Come.
[Exeunt all but ENOBARBUS and MENAS.]
MENAS.
[Aside.] Your father, Pompey, would never have made this treaty. —
You and I have known each other, sir.
ENOBARBUS. At sea, I think.
MENAS. We have, sir.
ENOBARBUS. You have done well by water.
MENAS. And you by land.
ENOBARBUS. I'll praise any man who'll praise me — though it can't be denied what I have done by land.
MENAS. Nor what I have done by water.
ENOBARBUS. Yes, something you can deny for your own safety: you have been a great thief by sea.
MENAS. And you by land.
ENOBARBUS. There I deny my land service. But give me your hand, Menas. If our eyes had authority, here they might arrest two thieves kissing.
MENAS. All men's faces are honest, whatever their hands are.
ENOBARBUS. But there's never a fair woman who has an honest face.
MENAS. No slander there. They steal hearts.
ENOBARBUS. We came here to fight you.
MENAS. For my part, I'm sorry it has turned into a drinking. Pompey is laughing his fortune away today.
ENOBARBUS. If he does, he certainly can't weep it back again.
MENAS. You've said it, sir. We didn't expect Mark Antony here. Tell me, is he married to Cleopatra?
ENOBARBUS. Caesar's sister is called Octavia.
MENAS. True, sir. She was the wife of Caius Marcellus.
ENOBARBUS. But she is now the wife of Marcus Antonius.
MENAS. Really, sir?
ENOBARBUS. It's true.
MENAS. Then Caesar and he are forever knit together.
ENOBARBUS. If I were forced to predict from this alliance, I would not prophesy so.
MENAS. I think policy played more part in the marriage than the love of the parties.
ENOBARBUS. I think so too. But you'll find the band that seems to tie their friendship together will be the very strangler of their friendship. Octavia is of a holy, cold, and quiet disposition.
MENAS. Who wouldn't want his wife to be so?

ENOBARBUS. Not the man who himself is not — which is Mark Antony. He'll return to his Egyptian dish. Then the sighs of Octavia will blow up the fire in Caesar, and, as I said before, what is the strength of their friendship will prove the immediate author of their quarrel. Antony will direct his affection where it lies. He only married his opportunity here.
MENAS. And so it may be. Come, sir, will you go aboard? I have a toast for you.
ENOBARBUS. I shall take it, sir. We've worked our throats in Egypt.
MENAS. Come, let's be off.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 7 — On board Pompey’s Galley, lying near Misenum
paragraphs: [Music. Enter two or three Servants with a banquet.]
FIRST SERVANT. Here they'll be, man. Some of their plants are ill-rooted already — the least wind in the world will blow them down.
SECOND SERVANT. Lepidus is flushed.
FIRST SERVANT. They've made him drink the leftovers.
SECOND SERVANT. As they pinch one another by the disposition, he cries out "no more," reconciles them with his entreaty, and himself to the drink.
FIRST SERVANT. But it raises a greater war between him and his discretion.
SECOND SERVANT. Why, this is what it is to have a name among the fellowship of great men. I'd rather have a reed that does me no service than a halberd I couldn't lift.
FIRST SERVANT. To be called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to move in it, is like being holes where eyes should be, which pitifully disfigure the cheeks.
[A sennet sounded. Enter CAESAR, ANTONY, POMPEY, LEPIDUS, AGRIPPA, MAECENAS, ENOBARBUS, MENAS with other Captains.]
ANTONY.
[To CAESAR.] This is how they do it, sir: they measure the flow of the Nile

by certain marks on the pyramid. They know by the height, the lowness, or the average whether dearth or plenty will follow. The higher the Nile swells, the more it promises. As it ebbs, the seedsman scatters his grain upon the slime and ooze, and soon comes to harvest.
LEPIDUS. You have strange serpents there?
ANTONY. Aye, Lepidus.
LEPIDUS. Your serpent of Egypt is bred from your mud by the operation of your sun — and so is your crocodile.
ANTONY. They are.
POMPEY. Sit, and bring some wine! A toast to Lepidus!
LEPIDUS. I am not as well as I should be, but I'll never quit.
ENOBARBUS. Not till you've slept. I fear you'll be in your cups till then.
LEPIDUS. No, certainly, I have heard that the Ptolemies' pyramises are very fine things. Without contradiction, I have heard that.
MENAS.
[Aside to POMPEY.] Pompey, a word.
POMPEY.
[Aside to MENAS.] Say in my ear, what is it?
MENAS.
[Whispers in his ear.] Leave your seat, I beseech you, captain,
and hear me speak a word.
POMPEY.
[Aside to MENAS.] Wait a bit. —
This wine for Lepidus!
LEPIDUS. What kind of thing is your crocodile?

ANTONY. It is shaped, sir, like itself, and it is as broad as it has breadth. It is just as high as it is, and moves with its own organs. It lives by what nourishes it, and when the elements are once out of it, it transmigrates.
LEPIDUS. What color is it?
ANTONY. Of its own color too.
LEPIDUS. It's a strange serpent.
ANTONY. It is. And its tears are wet.
CAESAR. Will this description satisfy him?
ANTONY. With the toast that Pompey gives him, or else he is a very epicure.
POMPEY.
[Aside to MENAS.] Go hang yourself, sir, hang! Tell me of that? Away!
Do as I bid you. — Where's this cup I called for?
MENAS.
[Aside to POMPEY.] If for the sake of my service you'll hear me,
rise from your stool.
POMPEY.
[Aside to MENAS.] I think you're mad.
[Rises and walks aside.]
What's the matter?
MENAS. I have always taken my cap off to your fortunes.
POMPEY. You've served me with much faith. What else is there to say? — Be jolly, lords.
ANTONY. These quicksands, Lepidus, keep off them — you'll sink.
MENAS. Will you be lord of all the world?
POMPEY. What do you say?
MENAS. Will you be lord of the whole world? That's twice now.
POMPEY. How could that be?
MENAS. Just entertain it. Though you think me poor, I am the man who will give you all the world.
POMPEY. Have you drunk well?
MENAS. No, Pompey, I have kept myself from the cup. You are, if you dare to be, the earthly Jove. Whatever the ocean encloses or the sky surrounds is yours, if you'll have it.
POMPEY. Show me how.
MENAS. These three world-sharers, these competitors, are on your ship. Let me cut the cable, and when we are out at sea, fall on their throats. Then all is yours.

POMPEY. Ah, you should have done this and not spoken of it! In me it would be villainy — in you it would have been good service. You must know that it is not my profit that leads my honor — my honor leads it. Repent that your tongue has so betrayed your action. Done in secret, I would have found it well done afterwards, but I must condemn it now. Stop, and drink.
MENAS.
[Aside.] For this,
I'll never follow your faded fortunes any more. Whoever seeks, and won't take when once it's offered, will never find it again.
POMPEY. This toast to Lepidus!
ANTONY. Carry him ashore. I'll pledge it for him, Pompey.
ENOBARBUS. Here's to you, Menas!
MENAS. Enobarbus, welcome!
POMPEY. Fill till the cup is hidden.
ENOBARBUS. There's a strong fellow, Menas.
[Pointing to the servant who carries off LEPIDUS.]
MENAS. Why?
ENOBARBUS. He bears the third part of the world, man. Don't you see?
MENAS. The third part, then, is drunk. I wish it all were, so that it might go on wheels!
ENOBARBUS. Drink, then. Increase the reeling.
MENAS. Come.
POMPEY. This isn't yet an Alexandrian feast.
ANTONY. It's ripening toward it. Sound the drums on the vessels, ho! Here's to Caesar!
CAESAR. I could well do without it. It's monstrous labor when I wash my brain and it grows fouler.
ANTONY. Be a child of the time.
CAESAR. Possess the time, I'd answer. But I would rather fast from everything for four days than drink so much in one.
ENOBARBUS.
[To ANTONY.] Ha, my brave emperor,
shall we dance now the Egyptian Bacchanals and celebrate our drink?
POMPEY. Let's have it, good soldier.
ANTONY. Come, let us all take hands until the conquering wine has steeped our senses in soft and delicate forgetfulness.
ENOBARBUS. All take hands. Pound our ears with the loud music while I place you. Then the boy shall sing. Every man shall beat the chorus as loud as his strong sides can volley.
[Music plays. ENOBARBUS places them hand in hand.]

THE SONG. Come, you monarch of the vine, plumpy Bacchus with pink eyes! In your vats our cares be drowned, with your grapes our hairs be crowned. Cup us till the world goes round, cup us till the world goes round!

CAESAR. What more do you want? Pompey, good night. Good brother, let me ask you to come away. Our graver business frowns at this levity. — Gentle lords, let's part. You see we have flushed our cheeks. Strong Enobarbus is weaker than the wine, and my own tongue splits what it speaks. The wild disguise has almost made fools of us all. What need of more words. Good night. Good Antony, your hand.
POMPEY. I'll test you on the shore.
ANTONY. And shall, sir. Give us your hand.
POMPEY. O Antony, you have my father's house. But — what? We are friends. Come, down into the boat.
ENOBARBUS. Take care you don't fall.
[Exeunt POMPEY, CAESAR, ANTONY and Attendants.]
Menas, I'm not going ashore.
MENAS. No, to my cabin. These drums, these trumpets, flutes! What! Let Neptune hear we bid a loud farewell to these great fellows. Sound, and be hanged, sound out!
[Sound a flourish with drums.]
ENOBARBUS. Hoo, he says! There's my cap!
MENAS. Hoo! Noble captain, come.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — A plain in Syria
paragraphs: [Enter VENTIDIUS as if in triumph, with SILIUS and other Romans, Officers and Soldiers; the dead body of Pacorus borne before him.]

VENTIDIUS. Now, darting Parthia, you are struck, and now pleased Fortune makes me the avenger of Marcus Crassus's death. Carry the king's son's body before our army. Your Pacorus, Orodes, pays this for Marcus Crassus.

SILIUS. Noble Ventidius, while your sword is still warm with Parthian blood, pursue the fleeing Parthians. Spur through Media, Mesopotamia, and the refuges where the routed flee. Then your grand captain Antony shall set you on triumphant chariots and put garlands on your head.

VENTIDIUS. O Silius, Silius, I have done enough. A lower man, mark well, may make too great an action. For learn this, Silius: better to leave a deed undone than by it acquire too high a fame when the one we serve is away. Caesar and Antony have ever won more through their officers than in person. Sossius, who held my place in Syria as Antony's lieutenant, for quick accumulation of renown — which he achieved by the minute — lost his favor. Whoever does more in war than his captain can do becomes his captain's captain; and ambition, the soldier's virtue, would rather choose loss than gain that overshadows him. I could do more to do Antony good, but it would offend him, and in his offense my achievement would perish.
SILIUS. You have, Ventidius, that without which a soldier and his sword scarcely deserve distinction. You'll write to Antony?

VENTIDIUS. I'll humbly report what we have accomplished in his name — that magical word of war: how, with his banners and his well-paid ranks, we have driven the never-yet-beaten Parthian cavalry exhausted from the field.
SILIUS. Where is he now?
VENTIDIUS. He intends to go to Athens, where we shall appear before him, with whatever haste the burden we carry will allow. — On there, pass along!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — Rome. An Ante-chamber in Caesar’s house
paragraphs: [Enter AGRIPPA at one door, ENOBARBUS at another.]
AGRIPPA. What, are the brothers parted?

ENOBARBUS. They've finished with Pompey — he's gone. The other three are sealing the agreement. Octavia weeps to part from Rome. Caesar is sad, and Lepidus, since Pompey's feast, as Menas says, is troubled with lovesickness.
AGRIPPA. He's a noble Lepidus.
ENOBARBUS. A very fine one. Oh, how he loves Caesar!
AGRIPPA. Yes, but how dearly he adores Mark Antony!
ENOBARBUS. Caesar? Why, he's the Jupiter of men.
AGRIPPA. What's Antony? The god of Jupiter.
ENOBARBUS. You spoke of Caesar? Why, he's nonpareil!
AGRIPPA. O, Antony! O you Arabian bird!
ENOBARBUS. If you'd praise Caesar, just say "Caesar" — go no further.
AGRIPPA. Indeed, he plied them both with excellent praise.

ENOBARBUS. But he loves Caesar best — yet he loves Antony. Hoo! Hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards, poets, cannot think, speak, cast, write, sing, number — hoo! — his love for Antony. But as for Caesar, kneel down, kneel down, and wonder.
AGRIPPA. He loves them both.
ENOBARBUS. They are his wing-cases, and he their beetle.
[Trumpets within.]
So, this is to horse. Adieu, noble Agrippa.
AGRIPPA. Good fortune, worthy soldier, and farewell.
[Enter CAESAR, ANTONY, LEPIDUS and OCTAVIA.]
ANTONY. No further, sir.

CAESAR. You take a great part of myself away with you. Treat me well in her. Sister, prove the kind of wife my thoughts make you, and as my farthest pledge shall stake on your good behavior. Most noble Antony, don't let the piece of virtue set between us — as the cement of our love to keep it built up — become the battering ram to attack its fortress. For we might have loved better without this go-between, if on both sides this isn't cherished.
ANTONY. Don't offend me with your distrust.
CAESAR. I have spoken.
ANTONY. You shall not find, though you look closely, the least cause for what you seem to fear. So may the gods keep you and make the hearts of Romans serve your ends. We'll part here.
CAESAR. Farewell, my dearest sister, fare you well. May the elements be kind to you and make your spirits all of comfort! Fare you well.
OCTAVIA. My noble brother!
ANTONY. The April is in her eyes. It is love's spring, and these are the showers to bring it on. — Be cheerful.
OCTAVIA. Sir, look well to my husband's house, and —
CAESAR. What, Octavia?
OCTAVIA. I'll tell you in your ear.
ANTONY. Her tongue will not obey her heart, nor can her heart inform her tongue — the swan's-down feather that stands upon the swell at the height of tide, and inclines neither way.
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside to AGRIPPA.] Will Caesar weep?
AGRIPPA.
[Aside to ENOBARBUS.] He has a cloud in his face.
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside to AGRIPPA.] He'd be the worse for that if he were a horse —
and so he is, being a man.
AGRIPPA.
[Aside to ENOBARBUS.] Why, Enobarbus,
when Antony found Julius Caesar dead, he cried almost to roaring; and he wept when at Philippi he found Brutus slain.
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside to AGRIPPA.] That year, indeed, he was troubled with a head cold;
what he willingly destroyed, he wailed over — believe it, until I weep too.
CAESAR. No, sweet Octavia, you shall hear from me still. The time shall not outrun my thoughts of you.
ANTONY. Come, sir, come, I'll wrestle with you in my strength of love. Look, here I have you — thus I let you go, and give you to the gods.
CAESAR. Adieu, be happy!
LEPIDUS. May all the number of the stars give light to your fair way!
CAESAR. Farewell, farewell!
[Kisses OCTAVIA.]
ANTONY. Farewell!
[Trumpets sound. Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS and ALEXAS.]
CLEOPATRA. Where is the fellow?
ALEXAS. Half afraid to come.
CLEOPATRA. Go on, go on.
[Enter a Messenger as before.]
Come here, sir.
ALEXAS. Good majesty, Herod of Jewry dares not look upon you except when you are well pleased.
CLEOPATRA. I'll have that Herod's head! But how, when Antony is gone, through whom I might command it? — Come closer.
MESSENGER. Most gracious majesty!
CLEOPATRA. Did you behold Octavia?
MESSENGER. Aye, dread queen.
CLEOPATRA. Where?
MESSENGER. Madam, in Rome I looked her in the face, and saw her led between her brother and Mark Antony.
CLEOPATRA. Is she as tall as me?
MESSENGER. She is not, madam.
CLEOPATRA. Did you hear her speak? Is she shrill-voiced or low?
MESSENGER. Madam, I heard her speak. She is low-voiced.
CLEOPATRA. That's not so good. He cannot like her for long.
CHARMIAN. Like her? O Isis! It's impossible.
CLEOPATRA. I think so, Charmian: dull of tongue and dwarfish! What majesty is in her gait? Remember, if you've ever seen majesty.
MESSENGER. She creeps. Her motion and her standing are as one. She shows a body rather than a life — a statue rather than a breathing thing.
CLEOPATRA. Is this certain?
MESSENGER. Or I have no powers of observation.
CHARMIAN. Three observers in Egypt could not give a better report.
CLEOPATRA. He's very knowing — I see that. There's nothing in her yet. The fellow has good judgment.
CHARMIAN. Excellent.
CLEOPATRA. Guess at her age, please.
MESSENGER. Madam, she was a widow.
CLEOPATRA. Widow! Charmian, listen!
MESSENGER. And I think she's thirty.
CLEOPATRA. Do you have her face in mind? Is it long or round?
MESSENGER. Round, almost to a fault.
CLEOPATRA. For the most part, too, those who are so are foolish. Her hair — what color?
MESSENGER. Brown, madam, and her forehead is as low as she would wish it.
CLEOPATRA. There's gold for you. You mustn't take my earlier sharpness badly. I'll employ you again. I find you most fit for business. Go ready yourself — our letters are prepared.
[Exit Messenger.]
CHARMIAN. A proper man.
CLEOPATRA. Indeed, he is. I much repent that I harried him so. Why, it seems to me, by his account, this creature is no great thing.
CHARMIAN. Nothing, madam.
CLEOPATRA. The man has seen some majesty, and should know.
CHARMIAN. Has he seen majesty? Isis forbid otherwise, after serving you so long!
CLEOPATRA. I have one more thing to ask him yet, good Charmian. But it's no matter — you shall bring him to me where I will write. Everything may be well enough.
CHARMIAN. I'll see to it, madam.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — Athens. A Room in Antony’s House
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY and OCTAVIA.]

ANTONY. No, no, Octavia — not only that. That would be excusable, that and a thousand more of similar import. But he has waged new wars against Pompey, made his will and read it to public ear, and spoken sparingly of me. When he was forced to give me terms of honor, he uttered them coldly and sickly. He extended me the narrowest measure. When the best opportunity was given him, he didn't take it, or did it through gritted teeth.

OCTAVIA. O, my good lord, don't believe everything — and if you must believe, don't stomach it all. A more unhappy lady, if this rift comes to pass, never stood between two sides praying for both. The good gods will mock me soon when I shall pray, "O, bless my lord and husband!" only to undo that prayer by crying just as loud, "O, bless my brother!" Husband win, win brother — each prayer destroys the other. There's no middle path between these extremes at all.

ANTONY. Gentle Octavia, let your best love draw to that side which seeks best to preserve it. If I lose my honor, I lose myself; better I weren't yours at all than yours so stripped of branches. But, as you requested, you yourself shall go between us. In the meantime, lady, I'll raise the preparation of a war that shall stain your brother. Make your soonest haste, so your wishes are still yours.

OCTAVIA. Thanks to my lord. May the Jove of power, weak as I am, very weak, make me your reconciler! Wars between you two would be as if the world should split, and only the bodies of slain men should solder up the rift.

ANTONY. When it becomes clear to you where this begins, turn your displeasure that way — for our faults can never be so equal that your love can move equally between them. Prepare for your going. Choose your own company, and command whatever cost your heart wishes.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — Athens. Another Room in Antony’s House
paragraphs: [Enter ENOBARBUS and EROS meeting.]
ENOBARBUS. How now, friend Eros?
EROS. There's strange news come, sir.
ENOBARBUS. What, man?
EROS. Caesar and Lepidus have made war upon Pompey.
ENOBARBUS. That's old news. What's the result?

EROS. Caesar, having used him in the wars against Pompey, immediately denied him equality. Wouldn't let him share in the glory of the action, and, not stopping there, accuses him of letters he had earlier written to Pompey. On his own complaint, he arrests him. So the poor third man is in chains, till death enlarges his confinement.
ENOBARBUS. Then, world, you have a pair of jaws, no more — and throw between them all the food you have, they'll grind one against the other. Where's Antony?
EROS. He's walking in the garden like this, and kicks the rush that lies before him. He cries, "Fool Lepidus!" and threatens the throat of his officer who murdered Pompey.
ENOBARBUS. Our great navy is rigged.
EROS. For Italy and Caesar. More, Domitius — my lord wants you immediately. I might have told my news later.
ENOBARBUS. It will come to nothing — but let it be. Bring me to Antony.
EROS. Come, sir.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — Rome. A Room in Caesar’s House
paragraphs: [Enter AGRIPPA, MAECENAS and CAESAR.]

CAESAR. Scorning Rome, he has done all this and more in Alexandria. Here's how it was: in the market-place, on a silvered tribunal, Cleopatra and himself in chairs of gold were publicly enthroned. At their feet sat Caesarion, whom they call my father's son, along with all the illegitimate offspring their lust has produced between them since then. To her he gave the establishment of Egypt — made her absolute queen of lower Syria, Cyprus, and Lydia.
MAECENAS. This in the public eye?

CAESAR. In the common showplace where they exercise. He proclaimed his sons there as the kings of kings: great Media, Parthia, and Armenia he gave to Alexander; to Ptolemy he assigned Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia. She appeared that day in the costume of the goddess Isis, and often before, it is reported, gave audience in the same way.
MAECENAS. Let Rome be informed of this.
AGRIPPA. The people, queasy from his insolence already, will withdraw their good thoughts from him.
CAESAR. The people know it, and have now received his accusations.
AGRIPPA. Whom does he accuse?

CAESAR. Caesar — saying that, having despoiled Sextus Pompeius in Sicily, we did not give him his share of the island. Then he says he lent me some ships, never returned. Lastly, he frets that Lepidus of the triumvirate should be deposed and, being so, that we hold all his revenue.
AGRIPPA. Sir, this should be answered.

CAESAR. It's done already, and a messenger gone. I've told him Lepidus had grown too cruel, that he abused his high authority and deserved his fall. Of what I have conquered, I grant him his share — but then in his Armenia and his other conquered kingdoms, I demand the same.
MAECENAS. He'll never yield to that.
CAESAR. Then neither must he be yielded to in this.
[Enter OCTAVIA with her train.]
OCTAVIA. Hail, Caesar, and my lord! Hail, most dear Caesar!
CAESAR. That I should ever have to call you castaway!
OCTAVIA. You haven't called me so, and have no cause to.

CAESAR. Why have you stolen upon us like this? You don't come like Caesar's sister. Mark Antony's wife should have an army for an usher, and the neighing of horses to tell of her approach long before she appeared. The trees along the way should have borne men, and expectation should have fainted from longing for what it didn't have. No, the dust should have ascended to the roof of heaven, raised by your populous troops. But you've come like a market-maid to Rome, and have prevented the ostentation of our love — which, left unshown, is often left unloved. We should have met you by sea and land, supplying every stage with an augmented greeting.

OCTAVIA. Good my lord, I wasn't compelled to come like this — I did it of my own free will. My lord, Mark Antony, hearing that you were preparing for war, informed my grieved ear of it, whereon I begged his pardon to return.
CAESAR. Which he soon granted, being an obstacle between him and his lust.
OCTAVIA. Don't say so, my lord.
CAESAR. I have eyes upon him, and his affairs come to me on the wind. Where is he now?
OCTAVIA. My lord, in Athens.

CAESAR. No, my most wronged sister. Cleopatra has nodded him back to her. He has given his empire over to a whore, and they are now levying the kings of the earth for war. He has assembled Bocchus, king of Libya; Archelaus of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, king of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king Adallas; King Manchus of Arabia; the King of Pontus; Herod of Jewry; Mithridates, king of Comagene; Polemon and Amyntas, the kings of Mede and Lycaonia, with a larger list of scepters still.
OCTAVIA. Oh, miserable me, with my heart divided between two friends who afflict each other!

CAESAR. Welcome here. Your letters did hold back our breaking forth, till we perceived both how you were misled, and how we were in negligent danger. Cheer your heart. Don't be troubled by the times that drive these strong necessities over your contentment, but let determined things hold their way unmourned, given over to destiny. Welcome to Rome, nothing more dear to me. You are wronged beyond the measure of thought, and the high gods, to do you justice, make their ministers of us and those who love you. Take the best comfort, and you are ever welcome to us.
AGRIPPA. Welcome, lady.

MAECENAS. Welcome, dear madam. Every heart in Rome loves and pities you. Only the adulterous Antony, most extreme in his abominations, turns you off and gives his potent army to a trull who clamors against us.
OCTAVIA. Is it so, sir?
CAESAR. Most certain. Sister, welcome. Please, be known forever for patience. My dearest sister!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 7 — Antony’s Camp near the Promontory of Actium
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA and ENOBARBUS.]
CLEOPATRA. I'll get even with you, don't doubt it.
ENOBARBUS. But why, why, why?
CLEOPATRA. You've spoken against my being in these wars, and say it isn't fitting.
ENOBARBUS. Well, is it, is it?
CLEOPATRA. Isn't war declared against us? Why shouldn't we be there in person?
ENOBARBUS. Well, I could reply: if we should serve with stallions and mares together, the stallions would simply be lost. The mares would each carry a soldier and his horse.
CLEOPATRA. What are you saying?

ENOBARBUS. Your presence must necessarily distract Antony — take from his heart, take from his brain, from his time, what shouldn't then be spared. He's already slandered for frivolity, and it's said in Rome that Photinus, a eunuch, and your maids manage this war.

CLEOPATRA. Let Rome sink, and their tongues rot that speak against us! We carry a share in the war, and as the head of my kingdom I will appear there as a man. Don't speak against it. I won't stay behind.
[Enter ANTONY and CANIDIUS.]
ENOBARBUS. No, I've finished. Here comes the Emperor.
ANTONY. Isn't it strange, Canidius, that from Tarentum and Brundusium he could so quickly cross the Ionian sea and take Toryne? — You've heard of it, sweet?
