CLEOPATRA. Speed is never more admired than by the negligent.
ANTONY. A good rebuke, which would have suited the best of men in taunting slackness. — Canidius, we will fight him at sea.
CLEOPATRA. At sea — what else?
CANIDIUS. Why does my lord do this?
ANTONY. Because he challenges us to it.
ENOBARBUS. And so my lord has challenged him to single combat.
CANIDIUS. Yes, and to fight this battle at Pharsalia, where Caesar fought with Pompey. But these offers, which don't serve his advantage, he shakes off — and so should you.

ENOBARBUS. Your ships aren't well manned. Your sailors are muleteers, reapers, people pressed into service in haste. In Caesar's fleet are men who have often fought against Pompey. Their ships are nimble, yours are heavy. No disgrace shall fall on you for refusing him at sea, being prepared for land.
ANTONY. By sea, by sea.

ENOBARBUS. Most worthy sir, you thereby throw away the absolute soldiership you have on land; distract your army, which mostly consists of war-marked footsoldiers; leave unused your own renowned knowledge; abandon the way that promises assurance; and surrender yourself merely to chance and hazard from firm security.
ANTONY. I'll fight at sea.
CLEOPATRA. I have sixty ships, Caesar none better.
ANTONY. We'll burn our extra shipping, and with the rest fully manned, from the headland of Actium beat back the approaching Caesar. But if we fail, we can still do it on land.
[Enter a Messenger.]
Your business?
MESSENGER. The news is true, my lord — he's been sighted. Caesar has taken Toryne.

ANTONY. Can he be there in person? It's impossible; strange that his forces should be. Canidius, you shall hold our nineteen legions by land, and our twelve thousand horse. We'll to our ship. Away, my Thetis!
[Enter a Soldier.]
How now, worthy soldier?

SOLDIER. O noble emperor, don't fight by sea. Don't trust to rotten planks. Do you doubt this sword and these my wounds? Let the Egyptians and the Phoenicians go ducking. We are used to conquering standing on the earth, and fighting foot to foot.
ANTONY. Well, well, away.
[Exeunt ANTONY, CLEOPATRA and ENOBARBUS.]
SOLDIER. By Hercules, I think I'm in the right.
CANIDIUS. Soldier, you are. But his whole action doesn't grow from the power that should drive it. So our leader is led, and we are women's men.
SOLDIER. You keep by land the legions and the horse intact, do you not?
CANIDIUS. Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius, Publicola, and Caelius are for sea, but we keep whole by land. This speed of Caesar's exceeds belief.
SOLDIER. While he was yet in Rome, his forces moved in such diversions as beguiled all spies.
CANIDIUS. Who's his lieutenant, do you hear?
SOLDIER. They say one Taurus.
CANIDIUS. Well, I know the man.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. The Emperor calls Canidius.
CANIDIUS. The time is in labor with news, and throws forth each minute some.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 8 — A plain near Actium
paragraphs: [Enter CAESAR with his army and TAURUS marching.]
CAESAR. Taurus!
TAURUS. My lord?
CAESAR. Don't strike by land — keep whole; don't provoke battle till we have finished at sea. Don't exceed the orders of this scroll. Our fortune depends on this throw.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 9 — Another part of the Plain
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY and ENOBARBUS.]
ANTONY. Set our squadrons on that side of the hill in view of Caesar's battle line, from which place we can observe the number of his ships, and so proceed accordingly.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 10 — Another part of the Plain
paragraphs: [CANIDIUS marches with his land army one way across the stage, and TAURUS, the Lieutenant of CAESAR, with his army the other way. After they have gone in, the noise of a sea fight is heard.]
[Alarum. Enter ENOBARBUS.]
ENOBARBUS. Lost, lost, all lost! I can't watch any longer. The Antoniad, the Egyptian admiral, with all their sixty ships, flee and turn the rudder. To see it has blasted my eyes.
[Enter SCARUS.]
SCARUS. Gods and goddesses — the whole assembled synod of them!
ENOBARBUS. What's your distress?
SCARUS. The greater portion of the world is lost through sheer ignorance. We have kissed away kingdoms and provinces.
ENOBARBUS. How does the fight look?

SCARUS. On our side, like the marked plague, where death is certain. That bawdy nag of Egypt, may leprosy overtake her — in the middle of the fight, when the advantage appeared like a pair of twins, both the same — or rather, ours the elder — the breeze upon her, like a cow in June, she hoists sails and flies.
ENOBARBUS. I saw it. My eyes sickened at the sight and couldn't endure another look.

SCARUS. Once she was turned away, the noble ruin of her magic, Antony, claps on his sea-wing and, like a doting mallard, leaving the fight at its height, flies after her. I never saw an action of such shame. Experience, manhood, honor, never before violated themselves so completely.
ENOBARBUS. Alas, alas!
[Enter CANIDIUS.]

CANIDIUS. Our fortune at sea is out of breath, and sinks most lamentably. If our general had been what he knew himself to be, it would have gone well. Oh, he has set the example for our flight most grossly by his own!
ENOBARBUS. Aye, are you of that mind? Well then, good night indeed.
CANIDIUS. They have fled toward the Peloponnesus.
SCARUS. It's easy to get there, and I will wait there to see what comes next.
CANIDIUS. To Caesar will I render my legions and my horse. Six kings already show me the way of yielding.
ENOBARBUS. I'll still follow the wounded fortune of Antony, though my reason sits in the wind against me.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 0 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY with attendants.]

ANTONY. Listen — the land bids me tread on it no more. It is ashamed to bear me. Friends, come here. I am so belated in the world that I have lost my way forever. I have a ship laden with gold. Take it, divide it. Flee, and make your peace with Caesar.
ALL. Flee? Not us.

ANTONY. I have fled myself, and have taught cowards to run and show their shoulders. Friends, be gone. I have resolved upon a course which has no need of you. Be gone. My treasure is in the harbor. Take it. Oh, I followed something I now blush to look upon. My very hairs mutiny — the white reprove the brown for rashness, and they reprove the white for fear and dotage. Friends, be gone. You shall have letters from me to some friends who will sweep your way for you. Please, don't look sad, or reply with reluctance. Take the hint my despair proclaims. Let what abandons itself be abandoned. To the seaside, immediately. I'll put you in possession of that ship and treasure. Leave me, please, a little — please, now. Yes, do so; for indeed I have lost my command. Therefore I beg you. I'll see you by and by.
[Sits down.]
[Enter CLEOPATRA led by CHARMIAN, IRAS and EROS.]
EROS. No, gentle madam, go to him! Comfort him.
IRAS. Do, most dear queen.
CHARMIAN. Do! Why, what else?
CLEOPATRA. Let me sit down. O Juno!
ANTONY. No, no, no, no, no.
EROS. Do you see her here, sir?
ANTONY. Oh, fie, fie, fie!
CHARMIAN. Madam.
IRAS. Madam — O good empress!
EROS. Sir, sir!

ANTONY. Yes, my lord, yes. He at Philippi kept his sword like a dancer's, while I struck the lean and wrinkled Cassius, and it was I who ended the mad Brutus. He alone worked through his lieutenants, and had no practice in the brave squares of war. Yet now — no matter.
CLEOPATRA. Ah, stand close.
EROS. The Queen, my lord, the Queen!
IRAS. Go to him, madam — speak to him. He's stripped of all his qualities by sheer shame.
CLEOPATRA. Well then, hold me up. Oh!
EROS. Most noble sir, rise. The Queen approaches. Her head is bowed, and death will seize her unless your comfort rescues her.
ANTONY. I have offended my reputation — a most ignoble swerving.
EROS. Sir, the Queen.
ANTONY. Oh, where have you led me, Egypt? See how I convey my shame out of your eyes by looking back at what I've left behind, destroyed in dishonor.
CLEOPATRA. O my lord, my lord, forgive my fearful sails! I little thought you would have followed.

ANTONY. Egypt, you knew too well that my heart was tied to your rudder by the strings, and that you would tow me after you. You knew your full supremacy over my spirit, and that your beckoning could command me, even against the bidding of the gods.
CLEOPATRA. O, my pardon!

ANTONY. Now I must send humble treaties to the young man, dodge and equivocate in the shifts of lowness — I, who played as I pleased with half the bulk of the world, making and marring fortunes. You knew how much you were my conqueror, and that my sword, made weak by my affection, would obey it for any cause.
CLEOPATRA. Pardon, pardon!

ANTONY. Don't shed a tear, I say — one of them outweighs all that's won and lost. Give me a kiss. Even this repays me. We sent our schoolmaster. Has he come back? Love, I am full of lead. Some wine in there, and our food! Fortune knows we scorn her most when she most offers blows.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 0 — Caesar’s camp in Egypt
paragraphs: [Enter CAESAR, AGRIPPA, DOLABELLA with others.]
CAESAR. Let the man who's come from Antony appear. Do you know him?
DOLABELLA. Caesar, it's his schoolmaster — an argument that he is plucked, when he sends here so poor a feather from his wing, when not many months ago he had superfluous kings for messengers.
[Enter Ambassador from ANTONY.]
CAESAR. Approach, and speak.
AMBASSADOR. Such as I am, I come from Antony. Until recently I was as petty to his purposes as the morning dew on the myrtle leaf to his great sea.
CAESAR. Be it so. Declare your office.

AMBASSADOR. The lord of his fortunes salutes you, and asks to live in Egypt. If that's not granted, he reduces his request, and begs you to let him breathe between the heavens and earth, a private man in Athens. That for him. Next, Cleopatra acknowledges your greatness, submits herself to your might, and asks of you the circle of the Ptolemies for her heirs — now hazarded upon your grace.

CAESAR. For Antony, I have no ears for his request. The queen shall not fail of audience or desire, so long as she drives her all-disgraced friend from Egypt, or takes his life there. If she does this, she shall not petition me unheard. So to them both.
AMBASSADOR. May fortune pursue you!
CAESAR. Bring him through the troops.
[Exit Ambassador, attended.]
[To THIDIAS.] Now it's time to try your eloquence. Hasten.

Win Cleopatra from Antony. Promise — in our name — whatever she requires; add more, by your own invention. Women in their best fortunes are not strong, but need will make the never-touched vestal perjure herself. Try your cunning, Thidias. Make your own edict for your pains, which we will answer as law.
THIDIAS. Caesar, I go.
CAESAR. Observe how Antony bears his fault, and what you think his every action speaks in every power that moves.
THIDIAS. Caesar, I shall.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 0 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, ENOBARBUS, CHARMIAN and IRAS.]
CLEOPATRA. What shall we do, Enobarbus?
ENOBARBUS. Think, and die.
CLEOPATRA. Is Antony or are we at fault for this?

ENOBARBUS. Antony only — who would make his will the lord of his reason. What if you did flee from that great face of war, whose ranks frightened each other? Why should he follow? The itch of his affection should not then have nicked his captainship, at such a moment, when half the world opposed half — with him being the central question. It was a shame no less than was his loss, to chase your fleeing flags and leave his navy staring.
CLEOPATRA. Please, peace.
[Enter the Ambassador with ANTONY.]
ANTONY. Is that his answer?
AMBASSADOR. Aye, my lord.
ANTONY. The Queen shall then have courtesy, so long as she yields us up.
AMBASSADOR. He says so.
ANTONY. Let her know it. — Send this grizzled head to the boy Caesar, and he will fill your wishes to the brim with principalities.
CLEOPATRA. That head, my lord?

ANTONY. Go back to him. Tell him he wears the rose of youth upon him, from which the world should note something particular: his coin, ships, legions, may be a coward's; whose officers would prevail under the service of a child as easily as in the command of Caesar. I dare him therefore to lay his fancy comparisons aside and answer me, on equal terms, sword against sword, ourselves alone. I'll write it. Follow me.
[Exeunt ANTONY and Ambassador.]

ENOBARBUS. Yes, it's likely the high-arrayed Caesar will give up his happiness and stage himself in a show against a swordsman! I see men's judgments are a part of their fortunes, and outward things draw the inward quality after them to suffer the same. That he should dream, knowing all measures, the great Caesar will answer his emptiness! Caesar, you have subdued his judgment too.
[Enter a Servant.]
SERVANT. A messenger from Caesar.
CLEOPATRA. What, no more ceremony? See, my women — against the blown rose may they hold their nose who knelt to the buds. Admit him, sir.
[Exit Servant.]
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside.] My honesty and I begin to fall out.
Loyalty well held to fools makes our faith mere folly. Yet he who can endure to follow with allegiance a fallen lord conquers him who conquered his master, and earns a place in the story.
[Enter THIDIAS.]
CLEOPATRA. Caesar's will?
THIDIAS. Hear it apart.
CLEOPATRA. None but friends here. Speak boldly.
THIDIAS. Perhaps they are friends to Antony.

ENOBARBUS. He needs as many friends, sir, as Caesar has — or he doesn't need us. If Caesar please, our master will leap to be his friend. As for us, you know whose he is, we are — and that's Caesar's.
THIDIAS. So. — Thus then, you most renowned: Caesar asks you not to consider in what condition you stand further than that he is Caesar.
CLEOPATRA. Go on; truly royal.
THIDIAS. He knows that you embrace not Antony in love, but in fear of him.
CLEOPATRA. Oh!
THIDIAS. The scars upon your honor, therefore, he pities as forced blemishes — not as deserved.
CLEOPATRA. He is a god, and knows what is most right. My honor was not yielded, but conquered outright.
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside.] To be sure of that,
I'll ask Antony. Sir, sir, you are so leaky that we must leave you to your sinking, for your dearest abandons you.
[Exit ENOBARBUS.]

THIDIAS. Shall I tell Caesar what you require of him? For he partly begs to be asked, so he can give. It would much please him that of his fortunes you should make a staff to lean upon. But it would warm his spirits to hear from me that you had left Antony and put yourself under his shroud — the universal landlord.
CLEOPATRA. What's your name?
THIDIAS. My name is Thidias.

CLEOPATRA. Most kind messenger, say to great Caesar this on my behalf: I kiss his conquering hand. Tell him I am ready to lay my crown at his feet and there to kneel. Tell him, from his all-commanding breath I hear Egypt's doom.
THIDIAS. It's your noblest course. Wisdom and fortune fighting together — if the former only dares what it can, no chance may shake it. Allow me to lay my duty on your hand.
CLEOPATRA. Your Caesar's father often, when he had thought of taking kingdoms in, bestowed his lips on that unworthy place as if it rained kisses.
[Enter ANTONY and ENOBARBUS.]
ANTONY. Favors, by Jove who thunders! What are you, fellow?
THIDIAS. One who simply performs the bidding of the fullest man, and worthiest to have command obeyed.
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside.] You'll be whipped.

ANTONY. Approach, there. — Ah, you kite! — Now, gods and devils, authority melts from me. Lately when I cried "Ho!" like boys to a scramble, kings would start forth and cry, "Your will?" Have you no ears? I am Antony yet.
[Enter Servants.]
Take this jack away and whip him.
ENOBARBUS. It's better to play with a lion's whelp than with an old one dying.

ANTONY. Moon and stars! Whip him. If they were twenty of the greatest tributaries who acknowledge Caesar, should I find them so saucy with the hand of her here — what's her name since she was Cleopatra? Whip him, fellows, till you see him cringe his face like a boy and whine aloud for mercy. Take him away.
THIDIAS. Mark Antony—
ANTONY. Drag him away. When he's whipped, bring him back. This jack of Caesar's shall carry us an errand to him.
[Exeunt Servants with THIDIAS.]

You were half blasted before I knew you. Ha! Have I left my pillow unpressed in Rome, gone without getting a lawful race of children — and by a gem of women — to be abused by one who fawns on feeders?
CLEOPATRA. Good my lord—

ANTONY. You have always been wavering. But when in our viciousness we grow hard — O misery of it! — the wise gods seal our eyes, drop our clear judgments into our own filth, make us adore our errors, laugh at us while we strut to our confusion.
CLEOPATRA. Oh, has it come to this?

ANTONY. I found you as a morsel cold upon dead Caesar's trencher; no, you were a fragment of Gneius Pompey's, besides what hotter hours you have luxuriously chosen, unregistered in common fame. For I am sure, though you can guess what temperance should be, you don't know what it is.
CLEOPATRA. Why this?

ANTONY. To let a fellow who'll take tips and say "God reward you!" be familiar with my playfellow — your hand, this kingly seal, and pledger of high hearts! O that I were upon the hill of Bashan, to outroar the horned herd! For I have savage cause, and to proclaim it civilly would be like a haltered neck that thanks the hangman for being quick about him.
[Enter a Servant with THIDIAS.]
Has he been whipped?
SERVANT. Soundly, my lord.
ANTONY. Did he cry? And beg pardon?
SERVANT. He did ask for mercy.

ANTONY. If your father lives, let him repent that you weren't made his daughter; and be sorry to follow Caesar in his triumph, since you've been whipped for following him. From now on, let the white hand of a lady give you fever; tremble to look on it. Get back to Caesar — tell him how you were treated. Be sure to say he makes me angry with him; for he seems proud and disdainful, harping on what I am, not what he knew I was. He makes me angry, and now is the easiest time to do it, when my good stars that were my former guides have emptied their orbs and shot their fires into the abyss of hell. If he dislikes my speech and what's done, tell him he has Hipparchus, my freed slave, whom he may at pleasure whip, or hang, or torture as he likes, to even the score with me. Press it home. Off with your stripes — be gone.
[Exit THIDIAS.]
CLEOPATRA. Are you done yet?
ANTONY. Alas, our earthly moon is now eclipsed, and it portends nothing but the fall of Antony.
CLEOPATRA. I must wait out his time.
ANTONY. To flatter Caesar, would you exchange glances with one that ties his bootlaces?
CLEOPATRA. Don't you know me yet?
ANTONY. Cold-hearted toward me?

CLEOPATRA. Ah, dear, if I be so, let heaven engender hail from my cold heart and poison it at the source, and let the first stone drop in my neck — and as it dissolves, so dissolve my life! Let the next strike Caesarion, till, by degrees, the memory of my womb, together with all my brave Egyptians, by the melting of this pelleted storm, lie graveless, till the flies and gnats of the Nile have buried them for prey!

ANTONY. I am satisfied. Caesar is encamping in Alexandria, where I will oppose his fate. Our force by land has nobly held; our scattered navy too have knitted again, and float, threatening most sea-like. Where have you been, my heart? Do you hear, lady? If from the field I shall return once more to kiss these lips, I will appear in blood. I and my sword will earn our chronicle. There's still hope in it.
CLEOPATRA. That's my brave lord!

ANTONY. I'll be triple-sinewed, hearted, breathed, and fight maliciously. For when my hours were fine and lucky, men used to ransom their lives from me for jokes. But now I'll set my teeth and send into darkness all who stop me. Come, let's have one more gaudy night. Summon all my sad captains. Fill our bowls once more — let's mock the midnight bell.
CLEOPATRA. It is my birthday. I had thought to keep it modest, but since my lord is Antony again, I will be Cleopatra.
ANTONY. We will yet do well.
CLEOPATRA. Call all his noble captains to my lord.

ANTONY. Do so — we'll speak to them; and tonight I'll force the wine to peep through their scars. Come on, my queen, there's sap in it yet. The next time I fight, I'll make Death love me, for I will contend even with his pestilent scythe.
[Exeunt all but ENOBARBUS.]

ENOBARBUS. Now he'll outstare the lightning. To be furious is to be frightened out of fear, and in that mood the dove will peck the ostrich; and I see still a diminishment in our captain's brain restores his heart. When valor preys on reason, it eats the sword it fights with. I will seek some way to leave him.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Caesar’s Camp at Alexandria
paragraphs: [Enter CAESAR, AGRIPPA, and MAECENAS, with his army. CAESAR reading a letter.]

CAESAR. He calls me boy, and scolds as if he had the power to beat me out of Egypt. He has whipped my messenger with rods, dares me to personal combat — Caesar against Antony. Let the old ruffian know I have many other ways to die. Meanwhile, laugh at his challenge.
MAECENAS. Caesar must reckon, when one so great begins to rage, that he's hunted nearly to falling. Give him no breath now, but exploit his distraction. Anger never makes a good guard for itself.

CAESAR. Let our best officers know that tomorrow we mean to fight the last of many battles. Within our ranks there are, from those who served Mark Antony only recently, enough to bring him in. See it done, and feast the army — we have plenty for it, and they have earned the waste. Poor Antony!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY, CLEOPATRA, ENOBARBUS, CHARMIAN, IRAS, ALEXAS with others.]
ANTONY. He will not fight with me, Domitius?
ENOBARBUS. No.
ANTONY. Why won't he?
ENOBARBUS. He thinks, being twenty times in better fortune, he is twenty men to one.
ANTONY. Tomorrow, soldier, I'll fight by sea and land. Either I will live, or bathe my dying honor in the blood that shall make it live again. Will you fight well?
ENOBARBUS. I'll strike, and cry, "Take all."
ANTONY. Well said. Come on. Call out my household servants. Let's be lavish at our meal tonight. —
[Enter Servants.]
Give me your hand. You have been rightly honest — so have you, and you, and you, and you. You have served me well, and kings have been your fellows.
CLEOPATRA.
[Aside to ENOBARBUS.] What does this mean?
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside to CLEOPATRA.] It's one of those odd tricks which sorrow
shoots out of the mind.
ANTONY. And you are honest too. I wish I could be made into so many men, and all of you packed together into an Antony, that I might do you service as good as you have done.
ALL THE SERVANTS. The gods forbid!
ANTONY. Well, my good fellows, wait on me tonight. Don't stint my cups, and make as much of me as when my empire was your fellow too, and obeyed my command.
CLEOPATRA.
[Aside to ENOBARBUS.] What does he mean?
ENOBARBUS.
[Aside to CLEOPATRA.] To make his followers weep.

ANTONY. Tend to me tonight. Perhaps this is the end of your duty. Maybe you shall not see me again — or if you do, a mangled shadow. Perhaps tomorrow you'll serve another master. I look on you as one taking his leave. My honest friends, I do not turn you away, but, like a master married to your good service, stay till death. Tend to me tonight for two hours, I ask no more, and may the gods reward you for it!
ENOBARBUS. What do you mean, sir, by giving them this discomfort? Look, they weep — and I, an ass, am onion-eyed. For shame, don't transform us into women.

ANTONY. Ho, ho, ho! Now the witch take me if I meant it that way! May grace grow where those drops fall! My hearty friends, you take my meaning in too sorrowful a sense, for I spoke to you for your comfort — I wanted you to burn this night with torches. Know, my hearts, I hope well of tomorrow, and will lead you where I expect victorious life rather than death and honor. Let's to supper, come, and drown all reflection.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Alexandria. Before the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter a Company of Soldiers.]
FIRST SOLDIER. Brother, good night. Tomorrow is the day.
SECOND SOLDIER. It will decide one way or the other. Fare you well. Did you hear of anything strange about the streets?
FIRST SOLDIER. Nothing. What news?
SECOND SOLDIER. Probably it's just a rumor. Good night to you.
FIRST SOLDIER. Well, sir, good night.
[Enter two other Soldiers.]
SECOND SOLDIER. Soldiers, keep careful watch.
THIRD SOLDIER. And you. Good night, good night.
[They place themselves in every corner of the stage.]
SECOND SOLDIER. Here we are. And if tomorrow our navy thrives, I have an absolute hope our landmen will stand firm.
FIRST SOLDIER. It's a brave army, and full of purpose.
[Music of the hautboys under the stage.]
SECOND SOLDIER. Quiet — what noise?
FIRST SOLDIER. Listen, listen!
SECOND SOLDIER. Hark!
FIRST SOLDIER. Music in the air.
THIRD SOLDIER. Under the earth.
FOURTH SOLDIER. It's a good sign, isn't it?
THIRD SOLDIER. No.
FIRST SOLDIER. Quiet, I say! What could this mean?
SECOND SOLDIER. It's the god Hercules, whom Antony loved, now leaving him.
FIRST SOLDIER. Walk. Let's see if other watchmen hear what we hear.
[They advance to another post.]
SECOND SOLDIER. How now, masters!
ALL. How now! How now! Do you hear this?
FIRST SOLDIER. Aye. Isn't it strange?
THIRD SOLDIER. Do you hear, masters? Do you hear?
FIRST SOLDIER. Follow the noise as far as our post allows. Let's see how it dies away.
ALL. Agreed. It's strange.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY and CLEOPATRA with others.]
ANTONY. Eros! My armor, Eros!
CLEOPATRA. Sleep a little.
ANTONY. No, my dear. — Eros! Come, my armor, Eros!
[Enter EROS with armor.]
Come, good fellow, put your iron on. If fortune is not ours today, it's because we defy her. Come.
CLEOPATRA. No, I'll help too. What's this for?
ANTONY. Ah, let it be, let it be! You are the armorer of my heart. Wrong, wrong. This, this!
CLEOPATRA. Truly, I'll help. This is how it must go.
ANTONY. Well, well, we shall thrive now. Do you see, my good fellow? Go put on your defenses.
EROS. Quickly, sir.
CLEOPATRA. Isn't this well buckled?

ANTONY. Excellently, excellently. He who unbuckles this — till we choose to take it off for our rest — shall hear a storm. You fumble, Eros, and my queen is a more skillful squire at this than you. Hurry up. O love, if you could see my battles today, and knew the royal occupation, you would see a workman at it.
[Enter an Officer, armed.]
Good morning to you. Welcome. You look like one who knows a warlike charge. To business we love, we rise early and go to it with delight.
OFFICER. A thousand, sir, early though it is, have on their riveted gear and at the gate expect you.
[Shout. Trumpets flourish.]
[Enter other Captains and Soldiers.]
CAPTAIN. The morn is fair. Good morning, general.
ALL. Good morning, general.

ANTONY. It's well started, lads. This morning, like the spirit of a youth who means to be of note, begins early. So, so. Come, give me that. This way. Well said. Farewell, dame. Whatever becomes of me, this is a soldier's kiss. [Kisses her.] It would be rebukable, and worthy of shameful check, to stand on more mechanical compliment. I'll leave you now like a man of steel. — You who will fight, follow me close, I'll bring you to it. Adieu.
[Exeunt ANTONY, EROS, Captains and Soldiers.]
CHARMIAN. Please, retire to your chamber.
CLEOPATRA. Lead me. He goes forth gallantly. If only he and Caesar could decide this great war in single combat! Then Antony — but now —. Well, on.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Antony’s camp near Alexandria
paragraphs: [Trumpets sound. Enter ANTONY and EROS, a Soldier meeting them.]
SOLDIER. May the gods make this a happy day for Antony!
ANTONY. If only you and those scars of yours had once prevailed in making me fight on land!
SOLDIER. Had you done so, the kings who have revolted, and the soldier who has left you this morning, would still have followed at your heels.
ANTONY. Who's gone this morning?
SOLDIER. Who? One ever near you. Call for Enobarbus — he won't hear you, or from Caesar's camp will say, "I am none of yours."
ANTONY. What are you saying?
SOLDIER. Sir, he is with Caesar.
EROS. Sir, his chests and treasure he didn't take with him.
ANTONY. Is he really gone?
SOLDIER. Most certain.

ANTONY. Go, Eros, send his treasure after him. Do it. Hold back not a jot, I charge you. Write to him — I'll sign — gentle adieus and greetings. Say that I wish he never finds further cause to change a master. Oh, my fortunes have corrupted honest men! Hurry. — Enobarbus!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Alexandria. Caesar’s camp
paragraphs: [Flourish. Enter AGRIPPA, CAESAR with ENOBARBUS and DOLABELLA.]
CAESAR. Go out, Agrippa, and begin the fight. Our will is that Antony be taken alive. Make it so known.
AGRIPPA. Caesar, I shall.
[Exit.]
CAESAR. The time of universal peace is near. If this proves a prosperous day, the three-cornered world shall bear the olive freely.
[Enter a Messenger.]
MESSENGER. Antony has come into the field.
CAESAR. Go, charge Agrippa to plant those who have revolted in the vanguard, so that Antony may seem to spend his fury upon himself.
[Exeunt CAESAR and his train.]

ENOBARBUS. Alexas did revolt and went to Jewry on Antony's business; there he dissuaded great Herod from inclining toward Caesar, and made him leave his master Antony. For this trouble, Caesar has hanged him. Canidius and the rest who fell away have employment but no honorable trust. I have done ill, for which I accuse myself so severely that I will know joy no more.
[Enter a Soldier of CAESAR's.]
SOLDIER. Enobarbus, Antony has sent all your treasure after you, with his bounty added. The messenger came up at my watch, and is at your tent now unloading his mules.
ENOBARBUS. I give it to you.
SOLDIER. Don't mock, Enobarbus. I tell you true. You'd best escort the bringer safely out of the host. I must attend to my duty, or would have done it myself. Your emperor continues still a Jove.
[Exit.]

ENOBARBUS. I am alone the villain of the earth, and feel that I am so most. O Antony, you mine of bounty — how would you have paid my better service, when my baseness you so crown with gold! This shatters my heart. If swift thought doesn't break it, a swifter means shall outstrike thought, but thought will do it, I feel. I, fight against you? No, I'll go seek some ditch in which to die — the foulest best suits the latter part of my life.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — Field of battle between the Camps
paragraphs: [Alarum. Drums and Trumpets. Enter AGRIPPA and others.]
AGRIPPA. Retire! We've engaged ourselves too far. Caesar himself is hard pressed, and our oppression exceeds what we expected.
[Exeunt.]
[Alarums. Enter ANTONY and SCARUS wounded.]
SCARUS. O my brave emperor, this is fought indeed! If we'd done so at first, we would have driven them home with rags about their heads.
ANTONY. You bleed fast.
SCARUS. I had a wound here that was shaped like a T — but now it's made into an H.
[Sounds retreat far off.]
ANTONY. They retreat.
SCARUS. We'll beat them into the privies. I have room yet for six more notches.
[Enter EROS.]
EROS. They're beaten, sir, and our advantage serves for a fine victory.
SCARUS. Let us score their backs and snatch them up as we take hares, from behind. It's good sport to maul a runaway.
ANTONY. I will reward you once for your spritely comfort, and tenfold for your good valor. Come, follow.
SCARUS. I'll limp after.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 8 — Under the Walls of Alexandria
paragraphs: [Alarum. Enter ANTONY again in a march; SCARUS with others.]

ANTONY. We have beaten him to his camp. Run one ahead and let the Queen know of our exploits. Tomorrow, before the sun sees us, we'll spill the blood that has escaped today. I thank you all, for you are doughty-handed, and have fought not just as men serving the cause, but as if each man's stake were as great as mine. You have shown yourselves all Hectors. Enter the city, embrace your wives, your friends; tell them your feats, while they with joyful tears wash the clotted blood from your wounds and kiss the honored gashes whole.
[Enter CLEOPATRA.]
[To SCARUS.] Give me your hand.

To this great fairy I'll commend your deeds — let her thanks bless you. O you day of the world, chain my armored neck. Leap, attire and all, through proof of armor to my heart, and there ride triumphing on the panting.
CLEOPATRA. Lord of lords! O infinite virtue, do you come smiling from the world's great snare uncaught?

ANTONY. My nightingale, we have beaten them to their beds. What, girl! Though grey is mixed with our younger brown, we still have a brain that nourishes our nerves, and can match youth goal for goal. Behold this man. Commend your favoring hand to his lips. — Kiss it, my warrior. He has fought today as if a god, in hatred of mankind, had destroyed in that shape.
CLEOPATRA. I'll give you, friend, an armor all of gold. It was a king's.

ANTONY. He has deserved it, even if it were jeweled like holy Phoebus's chariot. Give me your hand. Through Alexandria make a jolly march. Bear our hacked shields like the men who own them. If our great palace had the capacity to camp this host, we would all sup together and drink toasts to the next day's fate, which promises royal peril. — Trumpeters, with brazen din blast the city's ear; mingle with our rattling drums, so heaven and earth may strike their sounds together, applauding our approach.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 9 — Caesar’s camp
paragraphs: [Enter a Sentry and his company. ENOBARBUS follows.]
SENTRY. If we aren't relieved within this hour, we must return to the guardhouse. The night is bright, and they say we'll be drawn up in battle by the second hour of the morning.
FIRST WATCH. This last day was a sharp one for us.
ENOBARBUS. O, bear me witness, night. —
SECOND WATCH. Who is this man?
FIRST WATCH. Stand close and listen to him.
ENOBARBUS. Be witness for me, O blessed moon, when men who revolted shall on record bear hateful memory, that poor Enobarbus did repent before your face.
SENTRY. Enobarbus?
SECOND WATCH. Quiet! Listen further.

ENOBARBUS. O sovereign mistress of true melancholy, soak me in the poisonous damp of night, so that life, a very rebel to my will, may hang on me no longer. Throw my heart against the flint and hardness of my fault, which, being dried with grief, will break into powder and finish all foul thoughts. O Antony — nobler than my revolt is infamous — forgive me in your own private heart, but let the world rank me in the register as a master-leaver and a fugitive. O Antony! O Antony!
[Dies.]
FIRST WATCH. Let's speak to him.
SENTRY. Let's hear him — what he says may concern Caesar.
SECOND WATCH. Let's do so. But he sleeps.
SENTRY. Swoons rather, for so bad a prayer as his was never yet meant for sleep.
FIRST WATCH. Let's go to him.
SECOND WATCH. Awake, sir, awake! Speak to us.
FIRST WATCH. Do you hear, sir?
SENTRY. The hand of death has reached him.
[Drums afar off.]
Hark! The drums modestly wake the sleepers. Let's bear him to the guardhouse — he is of note. Our hour is fully out.
SECOND WATCH. Come on, then. He may yet recover.
[Exeunt with the body.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 10 — Ground between the two Camps
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY and SCARUS with their army.]
ANTONY. Their preparation today is by sea — we don't please them on land.
SCARUS. For both, my lord.

ANTONY. I wish they'd fight in the fire or in the air — we'd fight there too. But this is the way of it: our foot on the hills adjoining the city shall stay with us — orders for the sea are given. They have put out from the harbor — where we may best discover their arrangement and watch their effort.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 0 — Another part of the Ground
paragraphs: [Enter CAESAR and his army.]
CAESAR. But unless we are attacked, we'll stay still by land — which, as I judge, we shall, for his best force is out to man his galleys. To the valleys, and hold our best advantage.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 0 — Another part of the Ground
paragraphs: [Alarum afar off, as at a sea fight. Enter ANTONY and SCARUS.]
ANTONY. They aren't yet engaged. From where that pine stands, I shall discover all. I'll bring you word straight away how it's likely to go.
[Exit.]

SCARUS. Swallows have built their nests in Cleopatra's sails. The augurs say they don't know — they cannot tell. They look grim and dare not speak their knowledge. Antony is valiant and dejected, and by fits his frayed fortunes give him hope and fear of what he has and has not.
[Enter ANTONY.]

ANTONY. All is lost! This foul Egyptian has betrayed me. My fleet has yielded to the foe, and over there they throw their caps up and carouse together like friends long lost. Triple-turned whore! It is you who has sold me to this novice, and my heart wages war only on you. Bid them all flee, for when I am revenged upon my charm, I have done all. Bid them all flee! Be gone!
[Exit SCARUS.]

O sun, your rising I shall see no more. Fortune and Antony part here — even here we shake hands. All come to this! The hearts that fawned at my heels like spaniels, to whom I gave their wishes — they melt their sweets on blossoming Caesar, and this pine is stripped of bark that overtopped them all. Betrayed I am — O this false soul of Egypt! This deadly enchantress, whose eye beckoned forth my wars and called them home, whose bosom was my coronet, my chief aim — like a true gypsy at fast-and-loose, she has beguiled me to the very heart of loss. What, Eros, Eros!
[Enter CLEOPATRA.]
Ah, you spell! Be gone!
CLEOPATRA. Why is my lord enraged against his love?

ANTONY. Vanish, or I shall give you your deserving and blemish Caesar's triumph. Let him take you and hoist you up to the shouting plebeians! Follow his chariot like the greatest blot of all your sex; be shown like the worst monster for the lowest dwarfs, for fools — and let patient Octavia plough up your face with her prepared nails.
[Exit CLEOPATRA.]

It's well you're gone, if it's good to live — but it would be better if you fell into my fury, for one death might have prevented many. — Eros, ho! — The shirt of Nessus is upon me. Teach me, Alcides, my ancestor, your rage. Let me lodge Lichas on the horns of the moon, and with those hands that grasped the heaviest club, subdue my worthiest self. The witch shall die. She has sold me to the young Roman boy, and I fall under this plot. She dies for it. — Eros, ho!
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 0 — Alexandria. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS and MARDIAN.]
CLEOPATRA. Help me, my women! Oh, he is more mad than Telamon was for his shield. The boar of Thessaly was never so foaming with rage.
CHARMIAN. To the monument! Lock yourself in there and send him word you are dead. Soul and body do not part more painfully than greatness leaving us.

CLEOPATRA. To the monument! Mardian, go tell him I have killed myself. Say that the last word I spoke was "Antony," and word it piteously, please. Go, Mardian, and bring me word how he takes my death. — To the monument!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 0 — Alexandria. Another Room
paragraphs: [Enter ANTONY and EROS.]
ANTONY. Eros, you still see me?
EROS. Aye, noble lord.

ANTONY. Sometimes we see a cloud that's shaped like a dragon, a vapor sometimes like a bear or a lion, a towered citadel, an overhanging rock, a forked mountain, or a blue promontory with trees on it that nod to the world and mock our eyes with air. You have seen these signs. They are dark evening's pageants.
EROS. Aye, my lord.
ANTONY. That which is now a horse, even with a thought the drifting clouds dissolve and make it as indistinct as water is in water.
EROS. It does, my lord.

ANTONY. My good knave Eros, your captain is now just such a body. Here I am Antony, yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave. I made these wars for Egypt, and for the Queen, whose heart I thought I had — for she had mine, which while it was mine had annexed to it a million more, now lost. She, Eros, has stacked the cards with Caesar, and falsely played my glory away to an enemy's triumph. No, don't weep, gentle Eros. There's left us only ourselves to end ourselves.
[Enter MARDIAN.]
Oh, your vile lady! She has robbed me of my sword.
MARDIAN. No, Antony, my mistress loved you, and her fortunes were mingled with yours entirely.
ANTONY. Out, saucy eunuch! Peace! She has betrayed me, and shall die for it.

MARDIAN. The death of one person can only be paid once, and that she has discharged. What you would do is already done for you. The last words she spoke were, "Antony! Most noble Antony!" Then in the middle a tearing groan broke the name of Antony in two — it was divided between her heart and lips. She rendered up her life, your name so buried in her.
ANTONY. Dead, then?
MARDIAN. Dead.
ANTONY. Unarm me, Eros. The long day's task is done, and we must sleep. — That you depart from here safely repays your labor richly. Go.
[Exit MARDIAN.]

Off, pluck off! The sevenfold shield of Ajax cannot keep the battery from my heart. O cleave, my sides! Heart, for once be stronger than your container — crack your frail case! Quickly, Eros, quickly! No longer a soldier. Bruised pieces, go — you have been nobly borne. Leave me a while.
[Exit EROS.]

I will overtake you, Cleopatra, and weep for my pardon. So it must be, for now any length of time is torture. Since the torch is out, lie down, and stray no farther. Now every effort spoils what it does — yes, very force entangles itself with strength. Seal then, and all is done. Eros! — I come, my queen. — Eros! — Wait for me. Where souls lie down on flowers, we'll go hand in hand, and with our spritely bearing make the ghosts gaze. Dido and her Aeneas shall lack followers, and all the haunt shall be ours. — Come, Eros, Eros!
[Enter EROS.]
EROS. What would my lord?

ANTONY. Since Cleopatra died, I have lived in such dishonor that the gods detest my baseness. I, who with my sword quartered the world, and over green Neptune's back made cities of ships, condemn myself to lack the courage of a woman — to have a less noble mind than hers, who by her death tells our Caesar, "I am conqueror of myself." You are sworn, Eros, that when the moment of necessity should come — which now indeed has come, when I should see behind me the inevitable persecution of disgrace and horror — at my command you would then kill me. Do it. The time has come. You don't strike me — it's Caesar you defeat. Put color in your cheek.
EROS. The gods withhold me! Shall I do what all the Parthian darts, though hostile, lost their aim and could not?

ANTONY. Eros, would you be a spectator in great Rome and see your master like this, with his arms bound, bending his correctable neck, his face subdued to penetrative shame, while the wheeled chariot of fortunate Caesar, drawn before him, branded the baseness that followed?
EROS. I would not see it.
ANTONY. Come then — for I must be cured by a wound. Draw that honest sword of yours, which you have worn most usefully for your country.
EROS. Oh, sir, pardon me!
ANTONY. When I freed you, didn't you then swear to do this when I bade you? Do it at once, or your previous services are all but unpurposed accidents. Draw, and come.
EROS. Turn from me, then, that noble countenance in which the worship of the whole world lies.
ANTONY. There — look!
[Turning from him.]
EROS. My sword is drawn.
ANTONY. Then let it do at once the thing for which you have drawn it.
EROS. My dear master, my captain and my emperor, let me say, before I strike this bloody stroke, farewell.
ANTONY. It is said, man — and farewell.
EROS. Farewell, great chief. Shall I strike now?
ANTONY. Now, Eros.
EROS. Why, there then! [Kills himself.] Thus do I escape the sorrow of Antony's death.
[Dies.]

ANTONY. Thrice nobler than myself! You teach me, O valiant Eros, what I should do and you could not. My queen and Eros have, by their brave example, set up against me a nobleness in record. But I will be a bridegroom in my death, and run into it as to a lover's bed. Come then, and, Eros, your master dies your scholar. To do this
[Falling on his sword.]
I learned from you. How? Not dead? Not dead? The guard, ho! Oh, dispatch me!
[Enter a company of the Guard, one of them DERCETUS.]
FIRST GUARD. What's the noise?
ANTONY. I have done my work ill, friends. Oh, make an end of what I have begun.
SECOND GUARD. The star has fallen.
FIRST GUARD. And time is at its end.
ALL. Alas, and woe!
ANTONY. Let him who loves me strike me dead.
FIRST GUARD. Not I.
SECOND GUARD. Nor I.
THIRD GUARD. Nor anyone.
[Exeunt Guard.]
DERCETUS. Your death and fortunes bid your followers flee. This sword, shown to Caesar with these tidings, shall buy me entry with him.
[Enter DIOMEDES.]
DIOMEDES. Where's Antony?
DERCETUS. There, Diomed, there.
DIOMEDES. Is he alive? Won't you answer, man?
[Exit DERCETUS.]
ANTONY. Are you there, Diomed? Draw your sword and give me strokes enough for death.
DIOMEDES. Most absolute lord, my mistress Cleopatra sent me to you.
ANTONY. When did she send you?
DIOMEDES. Now, my lord.
ANTONY. Where is she?

DIOMEDES. Locked in her monument. She had a prophetic fear of what has come to pass. For when she saw — which shall never come to be — that you suspected she had made terms with Caesar, and that your rage could not be purged, she sent you word she was dead. But fearing afterwards how it might work, she sent me to proclaim the truth, and I have come, I dread, too late.
ANTONY. Too late, good Diomed. Call my guard, please.
DIOMEDES. What, ho! The emperor's guard! The guard, what ho! Come, your lord calls!
[Enter four or five of the Guard of ANTONY.]
ANTONY. Carry me, good friends, to where Cleopatra abides. It's the last service I shall command of you.
FIRST GUARD. Woe, woe are we, sir — you may not live to wear out all your true followers.
ALL. Most heavy day!

ANTONY. No, my good fellows — do not please sharp fate by gracing it with your sorrows. Welcome that which comes to punish us, and we punish it by seeming to bear it lightly. Take me up. I have led you often — carry me now, good friends, and have my thanks for all.
[Exeunt, bearing ANTONY.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 0 — Alexandria. A monument
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA and her maids aloft, with CHARMIAN and IRAS.]
CLEOPATRA. O Charmian, I will never go from here.
CHARMIAN. Be comforted, dear madam.
CLEOPATRA. No, I will not. All strange and terrible events are welcome, but comforts we despise. Our measure of sorrow, proportioned to our cause, must be as great as that which makes it.
[Enter, below, DIOMEDES.]
How now! Is he dead?
DIOMEDES. His death is upon him, but he is not dead. Look out of the other side of your monument — his guard have brought him there.
[Enter, below, ANTONY borne by the Guard.]

CLEOPATRA. O sun, burn the great sphere you move in! Let the varying shore of the world stand in darkness. O Antony, Antony, Antony! Help, Charmian! Help, Iras, help! Help, friends below! Let's draw him up here.
ANTONY. Peace! Not Caesar's valor has overthrown Antony — but Antony's own has triumphed on itself.
CLEOPATRA. So it should be, that none but Antony should conquer Antony — but woe that it is so!
ANTONY. I am dying, Egypt, dying. Only here I beg death to wait a while, until I lay upon your lips the poor last of many thousand kisses.

CLEOPATRA. I dare not, dear — dear my lord, pardon me. I dare not, lest I be taken. Not the imperious show of the full-fortuned Caesar shall ever be pinned with me. If knife, drugs, serpents have edge, sting, or effect, I am safe. Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes and quiet bearing, shall acquire no honor demurring at me. But come, come, Antony — help me, my women — we must draw you up. Assist, good friends.
ANTONY. Oh, quick, or I am gone.

CLEOPATRA. Here's sport indeed! How heavy my lord weighs! Our strength has all gone into heaviness — that makes the weight. If I had great Juno's power, the strong-winged Mercury should fetch you up and set you by Jove's side. Yet come a little — wishers were ever fools. Oh come, come, come,
[They heave ANTONY aloft to CLEOPATRA.]
and welcome, welcome! Die where you have lived; revive with kissing. If my lips had that power, I would wear them out so.
ALL. A heavy sight!
ANTONY. I am dying, Egypt, dying. Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.
CLEOPATRA. No, let me speak, and let me rail so high that the false housewife Fortune breaks her wheel, provoked by my outrage.
ANTONY. One word, sweet queen: of Caesar, seek your honor with your safety. Oh!
CLEOPATRA. They do not go together.
ANTONY. Gentle, hear me. Trust none about Caesar but Proculeius.
CLEOPATRA. My resolution and my hands I'll trust — none about Caesar.

ANTONY. Don't lament or sorrow over the miserable change now at my end — but please your thoughts by feeding them on my former fortunes, in which I lived the greatest prince of the world, the noblest; and don't die basely now, not cowardly take off my helmet to my own countryman — a Roman by a Roman valiantly vanquished. Now my spirit is going — I can do no more.
CLEOPATRA. Noblest of men, will you die? Have you no care for me? Shall I remain in this dull world, which in your absence is no better than a sty? O, see, my women,
[ANTONY dies.]

the crown of the earth melts. — My lord! O, the garland of war is withered, the soldier's pole has fallen; young boys and girls are level now with men. The greatness is gone, and there is nothing left remarkable beneath the visiting moon.
[Faints.]
CHARMIAN. O, quietness, lady!
IRAS. She is dead too, our sovereign.
CHARMIAN. Lady!
IRAS. Madam!
CHARMIAN. O madam, madam, madam!
IRAS. Royal Egypt, Empress!
CHARMIAN. Peace, peace, Iras!

CLEOPATRA. No more but even a woman, and commanded by such poor passion as the maid who milks and does the meanest chores. I should throw my scepter at the injurious gods — to tell them this world equaled theirs till they had stolen our jewel. All is nothing now. Patience is foolish, and impatience suits a dog that's mad. Then is it sin to rush into the secret house of death before death dares come to us? How are you, women? What, what! Good cheer! Why, how now, Charmian? My noble girls! Ah, women, women! Look — our lamp is spent, it's out! Good ladies, take heart. We'll bury him; and then, what's brave, what's noble, let's do after the high Roman fashion, and make death proud to take us. Come, away. This case of that huge spirit is now cold. Ah, women, women! Come — we have no friend but resolution and the briefest end.
[Exeunt, bearing off ANTONY's body.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Caesar’s Camp before Alexandria
paragraphs: [Enter CAESAR, AGRIPPA, DOLABELLA, MAECENAS, GALLUS, PROCULEIUS with his council of war.]
CAESAR. Go to him, Dolabella, bid him yield. Being so frustrated, tell him, he only mocks himself with the delays he makes.
DOLABELLA. Caesar, I shall.
[Exit.]
[Enter DERCETUS with the sword of ANTONY.]
CAESAR. Why is that? And who are you that dares appear thus to us?

DERCETUS. I am called Dercetus. I served Mark Antony, who was best worthy of being best served. While he stood up and spoke, he was my master, and I spent my life on his enemies. If you please to take me as your own, as I was to him I'll be to Caesar. If you don't please, I yield you my life.
CAESAR. What are you saying?
DERCETUS. I say, O Caesar, Antony is dead.

CAESAR. The breaking of so great a thing should make a greater crack. The round world should have shaken lions into civil streets and driven citizens into their dens. The death of Antony is not a single doom — in the name lay half the world.

DERCETUS. He is dead, Caesar, not by a public minister of justice, nor by a hired knife, but by that same hand which wrote his honor in the acts it did. With the courage which the heart lent it, it split the heart. This is his sword. I robbed his wound of it. Behold it stained with his most noble blood.
CAESAR. You look sad, friends. May the gods rebuke me, but this is news to wash the eyes of kings.
AGRIPPA. And strange it is, that nature must compel us to lament our most persistent deeds.
MAECENAS. His faults and honors were equally weighted in him.
AGRIPPA. A rarer spirit never steered humanity, but you gods will give us some faults to make us men. Caesar is moved.
MAECENAS. When such a spacious mirror is set before him, he must see himself.

CAESAR. O Antony, I have driven you to this, but we lance diseases in our bodies. I must necessarily have shown you such a declining day, or have looked upon yours. We could not be stalled together in the whole world. But yet let me lament with tears as sovereign as the blood of hearts, that you, my brother, my competitor at the top of every design, my mate in empire, friend and companion in the front of war, the arm of my own body, and the heart where mine kindled its thoughts — that our stars, irreconcilable, should divide our equalness to this. Hear me, good friends —
[Enter an Egyptian.]
But I'll tell you at a more fitting time. The business of this man looks out of him — we'll hear him out. Where are you from?

EGYPTIAN. A poor Egyptian still. The queen, my mistress, confined within all she has — her monument — desires to know your intent, so she may prepare herself in advance for the way she's forced to take.
CAESAR. Bid her have good heart. She shall soon know from us, by some of ours, how honorably and how kindly we determine for her. For Caesar cannot incline to be ungentle.
EGYPTIAN. So the gods preserve you!
[Exit.]

CAESAR. Come here, Proculeius. Go and say we purpose her no shame. Give her whatever comforts the quality of her passion shall require, so that, in her greatness, she doesn't defeat us by some mortal stroke. For her life in Rome would be eternal in our triumph. Go, and with all speed bring us what she says, and how you find her.
PROCULEIUS. Caesar, I shall.
[Exit PROCULEIUS.]
CAESAR. Gallus, go you along.
[Exit GALLUS.]
Where's Dolabella, to second Proculeius?
ALL. Dolabella!

CAESAR. Let him alone — for I remember now how he's employed. He shall be ready in time. Come with me to my tent, where you'll see how reluctantly I was drawn into this war, how calm and gentle I always proceeded in all my correspondence. Come with me, and see what I can show you in this.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Alexandria. A Room in the Monument
paragraphs: [Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN and IRAS.]

CLEOPATRA. My desolation does begin to make a better life. It is paltry to be Caesar. Not being Fortune, he's but Fortune's knave, a minister of her will. And it is great to do that thing which ends all other deeds, which shackles accidents and bolts up change, which sleeps and never tastes the dung again — the nurse alike of beggar and of Caesar.
[Enter PROCULEIUS.]
PROCULEIUS. Caesar sends greetings to the queen of Egypt, and bids you study on what fair demands you mean to have him grant you.
CLEOPATRA. What's your name?
PROCULEIUS. My name is Proculeius.

CLEOPATRA. Antony did tell me of you, and bade me trust you — but I don't greatly care about being deceived, having no use for trusting. If your master would have a queen as his beggar, you must tell him that majesty, to keep decorum, must beg nothing less than a kingdom. If he please to give me conquered Egypt for my son, he gives me so much of my own that I will kneel to him with thanks.

PROCULEIUS. Be of good cheer. You have fallen into a princely hand — fear nothing. Submit your case freely to my lord, who is so full of grace that it flows over upon all that need. Let me report to him your sweet submission, and you shall find a conqueror that will pray for help in showing kindness, where he is knelt to for grace.
CLEOPATRA. Please tell him I am the vassal of his fortune, and I send him the greatness he has won. Hourly I learn a doctrine of obedience, and would gladly look him in the face.
PROCULEIUS. This I'll report, dear lady. Take comfort, for I know your plight is pitied by him who caused it.
[Enter GALLUS and Roman Soldiers.]
You see how easily she may be surprised. Guard her till Caesar comes.
IRAS. Royal queen!
CHARMIAN. O Cleopatra, you are taken, queen!
CLEOPATRA. Quick, quick, good hands.
[Drawing a dagger.]
PROCULEIUS. Hold, worthy lady, hold!
[Seizes and disarms her.]
Do not do yourself such wrong, who in this are relieved, not betrayed.
CLEOPATRA. What, of death too — which rids our dogs of suffering?
PROCULEIUS. Cleopatra, do not abuse my master's bounty by destroying yourself. Let the world see his nobleness well acted, which your death will never let come forth.
CLEOPATRA. Where are you, Death? Come here, come! Come, come, and take a queen worth many babes and beggars!
PROCULEIUS. O, restraint, lady!

CLEOPATRA. Sir, I will eat no meat; I'll not drink, sir. If idle talk should once be necessary, I won't sleep either. I'll ruin this mortal house, whatever Caesar can do. Know, sir, that I will not wait pinioned at your master's court, nor ever be chastised by the sober eye of dull Octavia. Shall they hoist me up and show me to the shouting rabble of censuring Rome? Rather let a ditch in Egypt be my gentle grave! Rather lay me stark-naked on the mud of the Nile, and let the waterflies blow me into a thing of horror! Rather make the high pyramids of my country my gibbet, and hang me up in chains!
PROCULEIUS. You extend these thoughts of horror further than you shall find cause in Caesar.
[Enter DOLABELLA.]
DOLABELLA. Proculeius, your master Caesar knows what you have done, and has sent for you. As for the queen, I'll take her under my guard.
PROCULEIUS. So, Dolabella, it pleases me best. Be gentle with her.
[To CLEOPATRA.] To Caesar I will speak whatever pleases you,
if you'll employ me to him.
CLEOPATRA. Say I would die.
[Exeunt PROCULEIUS and Soldiers.]
DOLABELLA. Most noble empress, you've heard of me?
CLEOPATRA. I can't say.
DOLABELLA. Surely you know me.
CLEOPATRA. No matter, sir, what I've heard or known. You laugh when boys or women tell their dreams. Isn't that your trick?
DOLABELLA. I don't understand, madam.
CLEOPATRA. I dreamt there was an Emperor Antony. Oh, such another sleep, that I might see another such man!
DOLABELLA. If it might please you—
CLEOPATRA. His face was as the heavens, and there were set a sun and moon, which kept their course and lighted the little O, the earth.
DOLABELLA. Most sovereign creature—

CLEOPATRA. His legs bestrode the ocean. His reared arm crested the world. His voice was tuned like all the harmonious spheres — when speaking to friends. But when he meant to quake and shake the orb, he was as rattling thunder. As for his bounty, there was no winter in it — it was an autumn that grew the more by being reaped. His delights were dolphin-like — they showed his back above the element they lived in. In his livery walked crowns and lesser crowns; realms and islands were as small coins dropped from his pocket.
DOLABELLA. Cleopatra—
CLEOPATRA. Do you think there was, or could be, such a man as this I dreamt of?
DOLABELLA. Gentle madam, no.

CLEOPATRA. You lie, up to the hearing of the gods! But if there be — or ever were — one such, it is past the size of dreaming. Nature wants stuff to vie with fancy in strange forms. Yet to imagine an Antony would be nature's masterpiece against fancy, condemning shadows utterly.

DOLABELLA. Hear me, good madam. Your loss is, like yourself, great — and you bear it answering to its weight. May I never overtake pursued success, but I feel, by the rebound of yours, a grief that strikes my very heart at the root.
CLEOPATRA. I thank you, sir. Do you know what Caesar means to do with me?
DOLABELLA. I'm reluctant to tell you what I wish you knew.
CLEOPATRA. No, please, sir.
DOLABELLA. Though he be honorable—
CLEOPATRA. He'll lead me in triumph, then.
DOLABELLA. Madam, he will. I know it.
[Flourish. Enter CAESAR, PROCULEIUS, GALLUS, MAECENAS and others of his train.]
ALL. Make way there! Caesar!
CAESAR. Which is the Queen of Egypt?
DOLABELLA. It is the Emperor, madam.
[CLEOPATRA kneels.]
CAESAR. Arise — you shall not kneel. I pray you, rise. Rise, Egypt.
CLEOPATRA. Sir, the gods will have it thus. My master and my lord I must obey.
CAESAR. Don't trouble yourself with hard thoughts. The record of what injuries you did us, though written in our flesh, we shall remember as things done only by chance.
CLEOPATRA. Sole sir of the world, I cannot project my own case so well as to make it clear — but I confess I have been laden with the same frailties which before have often shamed our sex.

CAESAR. Cleopatra, know we will lessen rather than enforce. If you apply yourself to our intentions, which toward you are most gentle, you shall find a benefit in this change. But if you seek to lay on me a cruelty by taking Antony's course, you shall deprive yourself of my good purposes, and put your children to that destruction which I'll protect them from if you trust in this. I'll take my leave.
CLEOPATRA. And you may, through all the world. It's yours, and we — your trophies and signs of conquest — shall hang in whatever place you please. Here, my good lord.
CAESAR. You shall advise me in everything concerning Cleopatra.
CLEOPATRA. This is the summary of money, plate, and jewels I possess. It is exactly valued, no petty items admitted. Where's Seleucus?
[Enter SELEUCUS.]
SELEUCUS. Here, madam.
CLEOPATRA. This is my treasurer. Let him speak, my lord — on his peril — that I have kept nothing for myself. Speak the truth, Seleucus.
SELEUCUS. Madam, I'd rather seal my lips than speak, at my peril, what is not true.
CLEOPATRA. What have I kept back?
SELEUCUS. Enough to purchase what you have declared.
CAESAR. No, don't blush, Cleopatra. I approve your wisdom in the act.

CLEOPATRA. See, Caesar! Oh, behold how pomp is followed! Mine will now be yours, and if we should exchange places, yours would be mine. The ingratitude of this Seleucus makes me wild. O slave, of no more trust than hired love! What — do you go back on me? You shall go back, I warrant you! But I'll catch your eyes though they had wings. Slave, soulless villain, dog! Oh rarely base!
CAESAR. Good queen, let us entreat you.

CLEOPATRA. O Caesar, what a wounding shame is this — that you, deigning to visit me here, doing the honor of your lordliness to one so meek, my own servant should add the sum of my disgraces by the addition of his envy! Say, good Caesar, that I have kept some lady's trifles, unimportant toys, things of such dignity as we present to ordinary friends with; and say I have kept some nobler token apart for Livia and Octavia, to induce their mediation — must I be exposed by one I have raised? The gods! It strikes me below the fall I have.
[To SELEUCUS.] Please go away,
or I shall show the embers of my spirit through the ashes of my misfortune. If you were a man, you would have mercy on me.
CAESAR. Forbear, Seleucus.
[Exit SELEUCUS.]
CLEOPATRA. Let it be known that we, the greatest, are wrongly judged for what others do — and when we fall, we answer for others' merits in our own name, and are therefore to be pitied.

CAESAR. Cleopatra, neither what you have reserved nor what you've acknowledged do we put on the roll of conquest. It is still yours — bestow it at your pleasure, and believe that Caesar is no merchant to drive a bargain with you over things that merchants sell. So be cheered. Don't make your thoughts your prisons. No, dear queen — for we intend so to dispose of you as you yourself shall counsel us. Eat and sleep. Our care and pity for you is so great that we remain your friend. And so, adieu.
CLEOPATRA. My master and my lord!
CAESAR. Not so. Adieu.
[Flourish. Exeunt CAESAR and his train.]
CLEOPATRA. He flatters me with words, girls — he flatters me with words, that I should not be noble to myself. But listen, Charmian!
[Whispers to CHARMIAN.]
IRAS. Finish, good lady. The bright day is done, and we are for the dark.
CLEOPATRA. Hurry back. I have spoken already, and it is provided. Go put it to haste.
CHARMIAN. Madam, I will.
[Enter DOLABELLA.]
DOLABELLA. Where's the Queen?
CHARMIAN. Behold, sir.
[Exit.]
CLEOPATRA. Dolabella!

DOLABELLA. Madam, as I swore to you when you commanded — which my love makes religion to obey — I tell you this: Caesar intends his journey through Syria, and within three days he will send you with your children on ahead. Make your best use of this. I have performed your wish and my promise.
CLEOPATRA. Dolabella, I shall remain your debtor.
DOLABELLA. And I your servant. Adieu, good queen. I must attend on Caesar.
CLEOPATRA. Farewell, and thanks.
[Exit DOLABELLA.]

Now, Iras, what do you think? You, an Egyptian puppet, shall be shown in Rome as well as I. Mechanic slaves with greasy aprons, rules, and hammers shall lift us up to view. In their thick breaths, rank with gross diet, we shall be clouded, and forced to drink their vapor.
IRAS. The gods forbid!

CLEOPATRA. No, it's most certain, Iras. Saucy lictors will grab at us like whores, and crude rhymers ballad us out of tune. The quick comedians will improvise us on stage and present our Alexandrian revels. Antony shall be brought drunk on stage, and I shall see some squeaking Cleopatra-boy play my greatness in the posture of a whore.
IRAS. O the good gods!
CLEOPATRA. No, that's certain.
IRAS. I'll never see it, for I'm sure my nails are stronger than my eyes.
CLEOPATRA. Why, that's the way to fool their preparation, and to defeat their most absurd intents.
[Enter CHARMIAN.]

Now, Charmian! Show me, my women, like a queen. Go fetch my best attires. I am again for Cydnus, to meet Mark Antony. Iras, go. Now, noble Charmian, we'll dispatch indeed; and when you've done this chore, I'll give you leave to play till doomsday. Bring our crown and all.
[Exit IRAS. A noise within.]
What's this noise?
[Enter a Guardsman.]
GUARDSMAN. Here is a rural fellow who will not be denied entry to your highness. He brings you figs.
CLEOPATRA. Let him come in.
[Exit Guardsman.]

What a poor instrument may do a noble deed! He brings me liberty. My resolution is set, and I have nothing of woman in me. Now from head to foot I am marble-constant. Now the fleeting moon is no planet of mine.
[Enter Guardsman and Clown with a basket.]
GUARDSMAN. This is the man.
CLEOPATRA. Withdraw, and leave him.
[Exit Guardsman.]
Have you the pretty worm of the Nile there, that kills and pains not?
CLOWN. Truly, I have him — but I would not be the party who should desire you to touch him, for his biting is immortal. Those who die of it seldom or never recover.
CLEOPATRA. Do you remember any that have died of it?

CLOWN. Very many, men and women too. I heard of one of them no longer ago than yesterday — a very honest woman, but somewhat given to lying, as a woman should not do, except in the way of honesty — how she died of its biting, what pain she felt. Truly she gives a very good report of the worm; but he who would believe all that they say shall never be saved by half that they do. But this is most fallible — the worm is an odd worm.
CLEOPATRA. Be gone. Farewell.
CLOWN. I wish you all joy of the worm.
[Sets down the basket.]
CLEOPATRA. Farewell.
CLOWN. You must remember this, look you — the worm will do his nature.
CLEOPATRA. Aye, aye, farewell.
CLOWN. Look you, the worm is not to be trusted but in the keeping of wise people, for indeed there is no goodness in the worm.
CLEOPATRA. Don't worry — it shall be looked after.
CLOWN. Very good. Give it nothing, I beg you — for it isn't worth feeding.
CLEOPATRA. Will it eat me?

CLOWN. You mustn't think me so simple that I don't know the devil himself will not eat a woman. I know a woman is a dish for the gods, if the devil doesn't dress her. But truly, these same whoreson devils do the gods great harm in their women — for in every ten that they make, the devils mar five.
CLEOPATRA. Well, get gone. Farewell.
CLOWN. Yes, truly. I wish you joy of the worm.
[Exit.]
[Enter IRAS with a robe, crown, etc.]

CLEOPATRA. Give me my robe. Put on my crown. I have immortal longings in me. Now no more shall the juice of Egypt's grape moisten this lip. Quickly, quickly, good Iras — quick. I think I hear Antony call. I see him rouse himself to praise my noble act. I hear him mock the luck of Caesar, which the gods give men to excuse their later wrath. Husband, I come! Now to that name let my courage prove my title! I am fire and air; my other elements I give to baser life. — So, have you done? Come then, and take the last warmth of my lips. Farewell, kind Charmian. Iras, long farewell.
[Kisses them. IRAS falls and dies.]

Have I the asp in my lips? Do you fall? If you and nature can so gently part, the stroke of death is as a lover's pinch — which hurts, and is desired. Do you lie still? If you vanish thus, you tell the world it isn't worth taking leave of.
CHARMIAN. Dissolve, thick cloud, and rain — that I may say the gods themselves do weep!
CLEOPATRA. This proves me base. If she first meet the curly Antony, he'll question her, and spend that kiss which is my heaven to have. — Come, you mortal wretch,
[To an asp, which she applies to her breast.]
with your sharp teeth, untie at once this intricate knot of life. Poor venomous fool, be angry and dispatch me. Oh, if you could speak, so I might hear you call great Caesar an unpolicied ass!
CHARMIAN. O eastern star!
CLEOPATRA. Peace, peace! Don't you see my baby at my breast, that sucks the nurse asleep?
CHARMIAN. O, break! O, break!
CLEOPATRA. As sweet as balm, as soft as air, as gentle — O Antony! — No, I will take you too.
[Applying another asp to her arm.]
Why should I stay—
[Dies.]

CHARMIAN. In this vile world? So, farewell. Now boast yourself, Death — in your possession lies a lass unparalleled. Downy windows, close, and golden Phoebus shall never again be beheld by eyes so royal! Your crown is awry. I'll mend it, and then play.
[Enter the Guard rushing in.]
FIRST GUARD. Where's the queen?
CHARMIAN. Speak softly. Don't wake her.
FIRST GUARD. Caesar has sent—
CHARMIAN. Too slow a messenger.
[Applies an asp.]
Oh, come quickly, dispatch! I partly feel you.
FIRST GUARD. Approach, ho! All is not well. Caesar has been beguiled.
SECOND GUARD. There's Dolabella sent from Caesar. Call him.
FIRST GUARD. What work is here, Charmian? Is this well done?
CHARMIAN. It is well done, and fitting for a princess descended from so many royal kings. Ah, soldier!
[CHARMIAN dies.]
[Enter DOLABELLA.]
DOLABELLA. How goes it here?
SECOND GUARD. All dead.
DOLABELLA. Caesar, your thoughts touch their effects in this. You yourself are coming to see performed the dreaded act which you so sought to prevent.
[Enter CAESAR and all his train, marching.]
ALL. A way there, a way for Caesar!
DOLABELLA. O sir, you are too sure an augurer. What you feared has been done.
CAESAR. Bravest at the last, she aimed at our purposes — and, being royal, took her own way. The manner of their deaths? I don't see them bleed.
DOLABELLA. Who was last with them?
FIRST GUARD. A simple countryman who brought her figs. This was his basket.
CAESAR. Poisoned then.
FIRST GUARD. O Caesar, this Charmian lived just now. She stood and spoke. I found her trimming up the diadem on her dead mistress. Trembling she stood, and on a sudden dropped.
CAESAR. O noble weakness! If they had swallowed poison, it would appear by external swelling — but she looks like sleep, as though she would catch another Antony in her strong toil of grace.
DOLABELLA. Here on her breast there is a vent of blood, and something swelled. The like is on her arm.
FIRST GUARD. This is an asp's trail, and these fig leaves have slime upon them, such as the asp leaves upon the caves of the Nile.

CAESAR. Most probable, that she died so — for her physician tells me she had pursued infinite experiments in easy ways to die. Take up her bed, and bear her women out from the monument. She shall be buried by her Antony. No grave upon the earth shall hold within it a pair so famous. High events as these strike those who make them; and their story is no less in pity than his glory which brought them to be lamented. Our army shall in solemn procession attend this funeral, and then to Rome. Come, Dolabella, see to high order in this great solemnity.
[Exeunt all.]
